$100M Money Models|Alex Hormozi.brief: What happens to cash between a customer's first purchase and their next one?
$100M Money Models|Alex Hormozi.synopsis: Hormozi arranges offers in the order a customer encounters them. He works through introductory deals, upgrades and recurring purchases to show how two businesses with the same product can collect cash at very different speeds.
$100M Money Models|Alex Hormozi.author: Alex Hormozi built Gym Launch with his wife, Leila. Paying to acquire gym customers before their fees came in made the timing of cash a practical concern.

100M Leads|Alex Hormozi.brief: A field guide to finding people who might actually buy.
100M Leads|Alex Hormozi.synopsis: Hormozi follows a lead from first contact to a sales conversation. He separates work a founder can do personally, such as contacting former customers, from advertising or referrals that can reach strangers.
100M Leads|Alex Hormozi.author: Alex Hormozi first had to fill his own gyms. Later he sold other gym owners a system for doing the same, which gave him a second market in which to test his methods.

100M Offers|Alex Hormozi.brief: How to put together an offer a customer can judge before buying.
100M Offers|Alex Hormozi.synopsis: Price is only one part of Hormozi's calculation. He asks what result a buyer wants, how soon they expect it and how much risk they carry if the product disappoints.
100M Offers|Alex Hormozi.author: Before co-founding Acquisition.com, Alex Hormozi sold customer-acquisition programs to gym owners. His running examples come from selling a result that owners could measure in memberships.

12 Rules for Life|Jordan B. Peterson.brief: Peterson uses twelve everyday rules to ask what a person owes themselves and other people.
12 Rules for Life|Jordan B. Peterson.synopsis: Advice about posture or telling the truth leads into discussions of resentment, responsibility and suffering. Peterson moves between clinical anecdotes, biblical stories and his own family life.
12 Rules for Life|Jordan B. Peterson.author: Jordan Peterson practiced clinical psychology and taught psychology at the University of Toronto. An early version of the rules appeared in an answer he wrote on Quora.

33 Strategies of War|Robert Greene.brief: Military history becomes a set of studies in timing, morale and misjudgment.
33 Strategies of War|Robert Greene.synopsis: Greene takes apart campaigns to examine how commanders read an opponent, lose control of a coalition or spend resources they cannot replace. He then draws parallels with civilian conflicts.
33 Strategies of War|Robert Greene.author: Robert Greene had already used historical episodes to examine power and seduction. Here the unit of study is a campaign, where one decision changes the choices available later.

48 Laws of Power|Robert Greene.brief: Forty-eight lessons in how people gain influence and lose it.
48 Laws of Power|Robert Greene.synopsis: Greene pairs episodes from courts and political life with his reading of the tactics involved. The gap between what a ruler says publicly and what an adviser can safely say in private runs through the book.
48 Laws of Power|Robert Greene.author: Robert Greene developed the book with book producer Joost Elffers. Historical anecdotes gave him a way to write about power at work without relying on contemporary office stories.

5 Types of People Who Can Ruin Your Life.brief: Eddy describes recurring patterns in disputes that escalate whatever the other person does.
5 Types of People Who Can Ruin Your Life.synopsis: The book follows five high-conflict personality patterns and the behavior a reader can observe. Its practical sections concern boundaries, communication and deciding when to seek help.
5 Types of People Who Can Ruin Your Life.author: Bill Eddy has worked as a family lawyer, mediator and clinical social worker. He wrote for people who find themselves in a dispute without the tools available to a professional mediator.

50 Scientifically Proven Ways to be Pers.brief: Small changes in a request can change how people answer it.
50 Scientifically Proven Ways to be Pers.synopsis: Fifty short cases examine persuasion in everyday settings. One hotel study asks whether guests reuse more towels when a notice describes what earlier guests actually did.
50 Scientifically Proven Ways to be Pers.author: Social psychologists Noah Goldstein and Robert Cialdini worked with persuasion practitioner Steve Martin to translate research findings into decisions a reader might face at work.

7 Strategies for Wealth & Happiness|Jim.brief: Rohn treats keeping a journal and keeping accounts as related habits.
7 Strategies for Wealth & Happiness|Jim.synopsis: The seven strategies connect personal goals with the way a person spends money and time. Rohn asks readers to put their intentions on paper so they can compare them with what they actually did.
7 Strategies for Wealth & Happiness|Jim.author: Jim Rohn made his career giving business seminars. The book keeps the direct, exercise-based form of advice he delivered to those audiences.

A Brief History of Time|Stephen Hawking.brief: Can time have a beginning, and what could tell us if it did?
A Brief History of Time|Stephen Hawking.synopsis: Hawking follows what happens when gravity brings matter to extremes, first in collapsing stars and then in theories of the early universe. Black holes give him a concrete puzzle. Quantum theory suggests they can give off radiation.
A Brief History of Time|Stephen Hawking.author: Stephen Hawking studied cosmology and black holes at Cambridge. He wrote for readers curious about the questions physicists ask who did not have the mathematics to read the research papers.

A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ti.brief: A LinkedIn experiment asks which acquaintances help people find new jobs.
A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ti.synopsis: Researchers examined changes to the people LinkedIn recommended as contacts and tracked subsequent job moves. Moderately weak ties proved especially useful on some measures, and the pattern differed across industries.
A Causal Test of the Strength of Weak Ti.author: Karthik Rajkumar and his coauthors used randomized variations in LinkedIn's recommendation system. That design helped them distinguish a connection's effect from the tendency of similar people to meet.

A Happy Pocket Full Of Money|David Camer.brief: Gikandi approaches wealth as a question of attention and belief.
A Happy Pocket Full Of Money|David Camer.synopsis: The book asks readers to examine what they imagine when they think about money. Its exercises in visualization come from a spiritual account of abundance and draw analogies with quantum physics.
A Happy Pocket Full Of Money|David Camer.author: David Cameron Gikandi wrote this as a work of spiritual self-help. The physics references are part of his philosophical argument about belief and prosperity.

A Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy|Dougl.brief: Arthur Dent leaves Earth just before a demolition crew destroys it.
A Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy|Dougl.synopsis: His friend Ford Prefect turns out to be a researcher for an interstellar travel guide. Hitching a ride puts Arthur in a universe where bureaucracy travels farther than human common sense.
A Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy|Dougl.author: Douglas Adams first wrote the story as a BBC radio comedy. The disembodied narrator and the guidebook entries survived the move to print.

A Random Walk Down Wallstreet|Burton G..brief: Malkiel asks how much an investor can learn from yesterday's stock prices.
A Random Walk Down Wallstreet|Burton G..synopsis: He puts chart reading and company analysis alongside the evidence for index investing. Historical bubbles give him cases where a persuasive story and a sound price were very different things.
A Random Walk Down Wallstreet|Burton G..author: Burton Malkiel was a Princeton economist when the book first appeared in 1973. He made the case for a low-cost market portfolio before ordinary investors could readily buy one.

A Short History of Nearly Everything|Bil.brief: Bryson follows the people who worked out how old the Earth is and what it is made of.
A Short History of Nearly Everything|Bil.synopsis: The narrative moves across geology, physics and biology through the instruments, rivalries and accidents behind the discoveries. A measurement often starts with someone noticing that the accepted answer cannot quite work.
A Short History of Nearly Everything|Bil.author: Travel writer Bill Bryson wanted to understand the science that school textbooks had made seem settled and remote. He interviewed scientists and visited the places where they worked.

AI Engineering|Chip Huyen.brief: A guide to building software around models that can give a different answer on every run.
AI Engineering|Chip Huyen.synopsis: Huyen follows a foundation-model application through evaluation, retrieval and deployment. The hard question comes early. What evidence would show that a new answer is better than the last one?
AI Engineering|Chip Huyen.author: Chip Huyen has built machine-learning systems and taught machine learning systems design at Stanford. She wrote this book as pretrained models were changing what an application team had to build itself.

Activate Your Brain|Scott G. Halford.brief: Halford connects everyday work habits with what happens to attention under stress.
Activate Your Brain|Scott G. Halford.synopsis: He explores how threat, reward and rest affect a working day. The exercises ask readers to change a concrete condition, such as leaving room to recover between demanding tasks.
Activate Your Brain|Scott G. Halford.author: Scott Halford works with leaders on communication and performance. He wrote the book to bring ideas from behavioral science into the kinds of decisions his workshop participants faced.

Algorithms to Live by|Brian Christian &.brief: Computer science offers a surprisingly practical way to think about when to stop looking.
Algorithms to Live by|Brian Christian &.synopsis: An apartment search introduces optimal stopping. A cluttered desk introduces caching. The authors show what an algorithm assumes before asking whether it belongs in a human decision.
Algorithms to Live by|Brian Christian &.author: Brian Christian writes about computing and human judgment. Tom Griffiths studies how people learn and make decisions, a question he approaches with computational models.

Antifragile|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.brief: Why do some things improve when exposed to disorder?
Antifragile|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.synopsis: Taleb distinguishes things that survive a shock from things that gain from it. He examines small experiments, spare capacity and arrangements where the upside of an error differs from its cost.
Antifragile|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb spent years trading options, where exposure to a price change matters as much as the price itself. That asymmetry shapes his account of uncertainty.

Art of War|Sun Tzu.brief: An ancient Chinese treatise on winning a conflict at the lowest possible cost.
Art of War|Sun Tzu.synopsis: The text examines terrain, intelligence and the condition of both armies before battle. Some of its sharpest passages concern the commander who sees no reason to fight at all.
Art of War|Sun Tzu.author: Tradition attributes the text to Sun Tzu. Its exact authorship and date remain uncertain, and the surviving work belongs to the military literature of ancient China.

As We Speak|Peter Meyers & Shann Nix.brief: How much of a carefully prepared speech gets through to the person listening?
As We Speak|Peter Meyers & Shann Nix.synopsis: Meyers and Nix divide the work of speaking between content, delivery and the state of mind a speaker brings into the room. A well-written speech can still fail if listeners cannot follow its movement.
As We Speak|Peter Meyers & Shann Nix.author: Peter Meyers trained performers and public speakers. Journalist and broadcaster Shann Nix brought experience speaking to people who could turn the dial at any moment.

As a Man Thinketh|James Allen.brief: Allen uses the image of a garden to describe the thoughts a person tends.
As a Man Thinketh|James Allen.synopsis: This short essay follows his belief that repeated patterns of thought shape character and conduct. It belongs to the moral self-culture tradition of the early twentieth century.
As a Man Thinketh|James Allen.author: James Allen was an English essayist. He published this little book in 1903, long before habit formation became a subject of popular behavioral science.

Atomic Habits|James Clear.brief: Why is it easier to practice guitar when the instrument is already out of its case?
Atomic Habits|James Clear.synopsis: Clear follows a habit through the cue that starts it and the reward that brings you back. Moving a guitar into view changes the odds of picking it up tomorrow, even if your intentions stay much the same.
Atomic Habits|James Clear.author: James Clear developed the book through years of writing about habits. His account of rebuilding routines after a severe baseball injury gives the opening chapter its personal stakes.

Bad Blood|John Carreyrou.brief: The blood tests Theranos promised investors were a long way from the tests its machines could run.
Bad Blood|John Carreyrou.synopsis: Employees, patients and investors saw different pieces of the company. Carreyrou traces how secrecy kept them apart and how former staff helped establish what the technology could actually do.
Bad Blood|John Carreyrou.author: John Carreyrou broke the Theranos investigation for The Wall Street Journal in 2015. The book gave him room to reconstruct events that preceded his first story.

Becoming Steve Jobs|Brent Schlender & Ri.brief: How did the young executive pushed out of Apple become the person who led its return?
Becoming Steve Jobs|Brent Schlender & Ri.synopsis: The authors spend time in the intervening years at NeXT and Pixar. Those companies let them trace changes in Jobs's judgment and the people he learned to trust.
Becoming Steve Jobs|Brent Schlender & Ri.author: Brent Schlender covered Jobs for decades and interviewed him repeatedly. Rick Tetzeli joined him in revisiting that reporting and speaking to people who had worked closely with Jobs.

Beyond Order|Jordan B. Peterson.brief: Twelve further rules about what happens when familiar routines stop helping.
Beyond Order|Jordan B. Peterson.synopsis: Peterson takes up the dangers of excessive order, including avoiding necessary conflict and taking refuge in ideology. Clinical stories and readings of myths supply much of the argument.
Beyond Order|Jordan B. Peterson.author: Jordan Peterson wrote this follow-up after the public reception of his first rules book. The writing period also included serious illness in his family and his own prolonged health crisis.

Black Swan|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.brief: Taleb asks why the events that change history most are so easy to explain afterward.
Black Swan|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.synopsis: A rare event arrives outside the range of ordinary expectations. Once it happens, people assemble a story that makes it sound predictable. Taleb examines what that habit costs forecasters and investors.
Black Swan|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb traded derivatives before writing about probability for a general audience. In that work, a single extreme trading day could undo years of apparently reliable results.

Blitzscaling|Reid Hoffman & Chris Yeh.brief: When does it make sense for a young company to grow faster than it can organize itself?
Blitzscaling|Reid Hoffman & Chris Yeh.synopsis: Hoffman and Yeh examine companies racing to claim a market before a rival does. They trace the point at which the habits that helped a small team move quickly begin to fail.
Blitzscaling|Reid Hoffman & Chris Yeh.author: Reid Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn and invested in startups. Chris Yeh worked with early-stage companies, and the two developed these ideas in a Stanford course.

Born to Win|Zig Ziglar.brief: Ziglar starts with planning for a win, then asks how a person prepares for it.
Born to Win|Zig Ziglar.synopsis: Goals become a set of daily commitments. The book pays attention to the gap between wanting a particular outcome and having done enough preparation to expect it.
Born to Win|Zig Ziglar.author: Motivational speaker Zig Ziglar drew on his sales and speaking career. His son Tom worked with him on this account of the methods they taught.

Built to Sell|John Warrillow.brief: Could a buyer run your business after you walked away?
Built to Sell|John Warrillow.synopsis: In Warrillow's business fable, an agency owner wants to sell a company whose clients still depend on him personally. Turning one repeatable service into a product changes what a buyer is willing to pay for.
Built to Sell|John Warrillow.author: John Warrillow built and sold businesses before studying what made other owners' firms transferable. He chose a fictional agency so readers could follow a sale from the owner's side.

Burn the Boats|Matt Higgins.brief: Higgins asks when keeping an escape route makes a commitment harder to honor.
Burn the Boats|Matt Higgins.synopsis: He revisits decisions in which a fallback plan quietly absorbed time and attention. His cases include entrepreneurs as well as episodes from his own education and career.
Burn the Boats|Matt Higgins.author: Matt Higgins grew up in poverty in Queens, left high school and later became a sports executive and investor. Those early choices give his argument about commitment a personal history.

Business Habits that Drive High Performa.brief: Which everyday behaviors give a workplace its character?
Business Habits that Drive High Performa.synopsis: This shelf title points toward the authors' work on organizational culture. Their published book The Critical Few asks managers to choose a small number of observable behaviors and find the colleagues others already follow.
Business Habits that Drive High Performa.author: Jon Katzenbach, James Thomas and Gretchen Anderson worked on organizational culture at the Katzenbach Center. The exact publication behind this catalogue title is uncertain.

Business Model Generation|Alexander Oste.brief: A business model drawn on one page makes its assumptions easier to argue about.
Business Model Generation|Alexander Oste.synopsis: The Business Model Canvas puts customers, costs and revenue alongside partners and activities. The authors use worked examples to show what else must change when one part of a business changes.
Business Model Generation|Alexander Oste.author: Alexander Osterwalder developed the underlying framework through doctoral research supervised by Yves Pigneur. Practitioners contributed examples as the two turned it into a handbook.

Buy Back Your Time|Dan Martell.brief: Martell asks founders to look at their calendar before deciding whom to hire.
Buy Back Your Time|Dan Martell.synopsis: He starts with a time audit and follows the work an owner hands off. Documenting a task only pays off if someone else can actually do it without sending every decision back.
Buy Back Your Time|Dan Martell.author: Dan Martell founded software companies and later coached other founders. The book addresses a problem he encountered even in growing companies whose owners could afford help.

Can’t Hurt Me|David Goggins.brief: Goggins recounts the training, failures and endurance races through which he remade his life.
Can’t Hurt Me|David Goggins.synopsis: A difficult childhood and repeated setbacks precede his military training. Each chapter pairs a particular episode with a challenge drawn from the way he responded to it.
Can’t Hurt Me|David Goggins.author: David Goggins became a Navy SEAL and an ultradistance athlete. He wrote from the unusual position of having failed portions of training before eventually completing them.

Capital Returns|Edward Chancellor.brief: Today's best margins can pay for the factories that destroy tomorrow's.
Capital Returns|Edward Chancellor.synopsis: Marathon Asset Management's investment letters follow capital into popular industries and back out of neglected ones. New factories and fresh competition can destroy the margins that attracted investors in the first place.
Capital Returns|Edward Chancellor.author: Financial historian Edward Chancellor edited the collection. The investment arguments are the work of Marathon's managers, written as they assessed businesses for their portfolios.

Cashvertising|Drew Eric Whitman.brief: Whitman takes an advertisement apart to see what earns a reader's next few seconds.
Cashvertising|Drew Eric Whitman.synopsis: The book examines headlines, proof and the reasons a buyer might hesitate. Its examples come from direct response, where an advertiser can count the orders a piece of copy produces.
Cashvertising|Drew Eric Whitman.author: Drew Eric Whitman trained advertisers and wrote direct-response copy. He organized the book around choices a copywriter can make on the page.

Chinas Super Consumers|Savio Chan & Mich.brief: What happens when a Chinese shopper encounters a foreign brand at home and abroad?
Chinas Super Consumers|Savio Chan & Mich.synopsis: Chan and Zakkour examine changing household expectations, shopping habits and the meanings attached to brands. They write for businesses trying to understand a market that varies considerably by region and customer.
Chinas Super Consumers|Savio Chan & Mich.author: Savio Chan and Michael Zakkour advised companies doing business in China. Their account grew out of work connecting Chinese consumers with international retailers.

Company of One|Paul Jarvis.brief: How much business does an independent business owner actually want?
Company of One|Paul Jarvis.synopsis: He examines decisions about staffing, recurring costs and how much revenue counts as enough. Growth becomes a choice with a price the owner can calculate.
Company of One|Paul Jarvis.author: Paul Jarvis ran an independent design business. The book came out of his experience making a living from client work without building a conventional agency.

Confessions of an Advertising Man|David.brief: Ogilvy describes how he found clients and built an advertising agency they would keep.
Confessions of an Advertising Man|David.synopsis: Alongside advice on headlines and research are chapters on running the office and handling an account. A bad relationship with a client can ruin an otherwise good campaign.
Confessions of an Advertising Man|David.author: David Ogilvy published the book in 1963, while running the agency he founded on Madison Avenue. Earlier jobs in sales and audience research shaped his interest in evidence.

Content Inc.|Joe Pulizzi.brief: Pulizzi starts a business with a readership and asks what it might eventually sell.
Content Inc.|Joe Pulizzi.synopsis: The method begins with a narrow subject and a dependable publishing schedule. Revenue comes later, once the publisher knows who keeps coming back and why.
Content Inc.|Joe Pulizzi.author: Joe Pulizzi founded the Content Marketing Institute. His own trade publication and events business supplied a working example of the sequence he describes.

Copywriting Secrets|Jim Edwards.brief: Edwards shows how to write sales copy when you have a product and a blank page.
Copywriting Secrets|Jim Edwards.synopsis: He works through promises, headlines and objections in the order a potential buyer encounters them. The exercises ask the seller to name what a customer would gain in ordinary language.
Copywriting Secrets|Jim Edwards.author: Jim Edwards sold products online and taught entrepreneurs to write their own copy. He wrote this for business owners who normally have to do the selling themselves.

Courage Is Calling|Ryan Holiday.brief: Holiday examines the moment someone decides to act despite a foreseeable cost.
Courage Is Calling|Ryan Holiday.synopsis: Historical episodes let him distinguish an initial act of courage from the work of sustaining it. He pays particular attention to fear of public disapproval.
Courage Is Calling|Ryan Holiday.author: Ryan Holiday writes popular books on Stoicism. This volume opened his series on the four classical virtues, with courage as the first subject.

Cryptoassets|Chris Burniske & Jack Tatar.brief: A framework for examining a digital asset as an investor.
Cryptoassets|Chris Burniske & Jack Tatar.synopsis: Burniske and Tatar distinguish different kinds of cryptoassets and ask what could give each one value. They place the early trading history beside questions of custody, risk and portfolio construction.
Cryptoassets|Chris Burniske & Jack Tatar.author: Chris Burniske worked on cryptoasset research at ARK Invest. Jack Tatar brought a financial adviser's perspective to a book written while the asset class was still young.

Deep Work|Cal Newport.brief: What gets done in an uninterrupted morning that never gets done between emails?
Deep Work|Cal Newport.synopsis: Newport looks at how scholars and programmers protect time for difficult work. He describes several workable schedules, including a regular daily block for people who cannot disappear for weeks at a stretch.
Deep Work|Cal Newport.author: Cal Newport is a computer scientist. His own research requires long stretches of uninterrupted thought, and he wrote the book while digital communication was taking up more of the working day.

Devil Take the Hindmost|Edward Chancello.brief: A history of what people buy when they expect someone else to pay more tomorrow.
Devil Take the Hindmost|Edward Chancello.synopsis: Chancellor follows speculative episodes across centuries, including railway promotions and stock-market booms. He asks what each generation remembered about earlier crashes and what it managed to forget.
Devil Take the Hindmost|Edward Chancello.author: Edward Chancellor worked in finance before becoming a financial writer. He completed the book during the late-1990s market boom, while his historical subject had fresh counterparts.

Digital Minimalism|Cal Newport.brief: Which digital tools would you invite back after a month without them?
Digital Minimalism|Cal Newport.synopsis: Newport proposes a temporary break from optional technologies. Reintroducing them one at a time makes it easier to see which activities they support and which activities they displace.
Digital Minimalism|Cal Newport.author: Computer scientist Cal Newport wrote this after hearing from readers who felt attached to their phones even outside work, a problem his earlier book on concentration only partly addressed.

Discipline Equals Freedom Field Manual|J.brief: Willink lays out the routines he uses when motivation is in short supply.
Discipline Equals Freedom Field Manual|J.synopsis: Short entries cover training, sleep and the arguments people make with themselves before starting. The field-manual format lets a reader turn directly to the obstacle at hand.
Discipline Equals Freedom Field Manual|J.author: Jocko Willink served as a Navy SEAL officer and commanded a task unit in Iraq. His account of discipline draws on military routines and the training he kept after service.

Discipline Is Destiny|Ryan Holiday.brief: Holiday studies restraint through the lives of people who wielded unusual power.
Discipline Is Destiny|Ryan Holiday.synopsis: Examples of athletic training sit next to accounts of leaders who had every opportunity to overindulge. The recurring question is what a person can govern when nobody else can tell them no.
Discipline Is Destiny|Ryan Holiday.author: Ryan Holiday wrote this second volume of his classical virtues series about temperance. His interest in Stoicism shapes his choice of examples.

Do Things That Don’t Scale|Paul Graham.brief: Stripe's founders used to install the software on a willing customer's laptop themselves.
Do Things That Don’t Scale|Paul Graham.synopsis: For a startup with a handful of users, personal attention does two jobs. It wins an early customer and lets the founders see exactly where that customer gets stuck. Graham describes what they learn by doing this work by hand.
Do Things That Don’t Scale|Paul Graham.author: Paul Graham co-founded Y Combinator. He wrote this 2013 essay after seeing founders hesitate to do small, laborious things that could get their companies started.

DotCom Secrets|Russell Brunson.brief: Brunson maps what happens between a stranger landing on a website and becoming a customer.
DotCom Secrets|Russell Brunson.synopsis: The book follows visitors through a sequence of pages and offers. Brunson shows how changing the order of those offers changes what a customer sees and what the seller can learn.
DotCom Secrets|Russell Brunson.author: Russell Brunson co-founded ClickFunnels, software for building these sales sequences. He wrote for sellers who needed to understand the sequence before choosing the software.

Economic Facts and Fallacies|Thomas Sowe.brief: Sowell takes apart economic claims that sound obvious on first hearing.
Economic Facts and Fallacies|Thomas Sowe.synopsis: Examples in housing, education and labor markets turn on the choice of comparison. A statistic can accurately describe two groups while giving a misleading account of why their outcomes differ.
Economic Facts and Fallacies|Thomas Sowe.author: Thomas Sowell was an economist and a Hoover Institution fellow. He wrote for general readers accustomed to encountering economic arguments through politics and the press.

Economics in One Lesson|Henry Hazlitt.brief: Hazlitt follows the cost of a policy past the people who benefit first.
Economics in One Lesson|Henry Hazlitt.synopsis: A broken window gives a glazier work, but the shopkeeper must give up another purchase. Hazlitt carries that line of reasoning into tariffs, wages and public spending.
Economics in One Lesson|Henry Hazlitt.author: Henry Hazlitt was a financial journalist. He wrote the book in the 1940s in the tradition of Frédéric Bastiat's essays on the visible and unseen effects of economic choices.

Elon Musk - Walter Isaacson|Walter Isaac.brief: A close account of how Musk makes decisions inside the companies he runs.
Elon Musk - Walter Isaacson|Walter Isaac.synopsis: Isaacson follows meetings on factory floors, rocket launches and the Twitter acquisition. Scenes of last-minute intervention let the reader observe how Musk's deadlines affect the people doing the work.
Elon Musk - Walter Isaacson|Walter Isaac.author: Walter Isaacson spent roughly two years shadowing Musk. That access puts the biography close to its subject during decisions the author could witness firsthand.

Elon Musk- Ashlee Vance|Ashlee Vance.brief: Vance follows Musk's path into electric cars and commercial spaceflight.
Elon Musk- Ashlee Vance|Ashlee Vance.synopsis: The biography moves through his early software ventures to the years when Tesla and SpaceX both faced the prospect of failure. Colleagues and former employees describe what it cost to keep them operating.
Elon Musk- Ashlee Vance|Ashlee Vance.author: Technology reporter Ashlee Vance interviewed Musk and people around him for a biography published in 2015. It captures a much earlier stage of the companies than Isaacson's later account.

Enterprise AI Startups are Rewriting the.brief: A venture firm's look at how quickly enterprise AI companies were finding paying customers in 2025.
Enterprise AI Startups are Rewriting the.synopsis: The newsletter compares early revenue growth with familiar software benchmarks. It asks what rapid adoption says about staying power when customers can still switch between competing products.
Enterprise AI Startups are Rewriting the.author: Andreessen Horowitz's enterprise team published this dispatch in July 2025. The authors write as investors in the market whose growth they are measuring.

Enterprise Sales for Founders|YC Startup.brief: What does a founder have to do before a large company will sign?
Enterprise Sales for Founders|YC Startup.synopsis: This YC lesson follows the enterprise sale beyond the product demonstration. A user who wants the software may still need to persuade a budget owner and get the purchase through procurement.
Enterprise Sales for Founders|YC Startup.author: Y Combinator publishes lessons for the founders it funds and for people building their first companies. Its enterprise sales material addresses teams that still rely on founders to close deals.

Entrusted|Frank Hanna.brief: A shelf entry about the responsibility that comes with family wealth. The edition is uncertain.
Entrusted|Frank Hanna.synopsis: One published title, Entrusted, examines what families pass on besides money. Frank Hanna also writes about stewardship, but the available publication records do not establish that the two works are the same.
Entrusted|Frank Hanna.author: The catalogue credits Frank Hanna, a businessman and philanthropist who wrote What Your Money Means. David York and Andrew Howell wrote Entrusted: Building a Legacy That Lasts.

Epictetus|Epictetus.brief: Epictetus asks where a person's freedom begins when circumstances refuse to cooperate.
Epictetus|Epictetus.synopsis: His teaching distinguishes what we can decide from what happens to us. A reputation, an illness or somebody else's anger offers a test of that distinction. This entry does not specify a particular collection.
Epictetus|Epictetus.author: Epictetus lived under slavery before teaching philosophy in the Roman world. His student Arrian recorded his teaching, which survives in the Discourses and a shorter handbook.

Exceptional|Daniel Cable.brief: Cable asks what other people remember about us when we are doing our best work.
Exceptional|Daniel Cable.synopsis: The book invites readers to gather accounts of particular moments from people who know them. Those stories can reveal abilities a performance review or a list of personal strengths might miss.
Exceptional|Daniel Cable.author: Daniel Cable teaches organizational behavior at London Business School. The book grows out of research into how people respond when others recognize a specific contribution they have made.

Expert Secrets|Russell Brunson.brief: How does someone turn specialist knowledge into something others will pay to learn?
Expert Secrets|Russell Brunson.synopsis: Brunson follows an expert through choosing an audience, explaining a method and making a sales presentation. Stories matter here because they help a potential buyer understand what is being offered.
Expert Secrets|Russell Brunson.author: Russell Brunson co-founded ClickFunnels. This book focuses on the teacher or presenter using a sales funnel, the human counterpart to the system in DotCom Secrets.

Fake|Robert T. Kiyosaki.brief: Kiyosaki challenges familiar beliefs about money, education and the assets people buy.
Fake|Robert T. Kiyosaki.synopsis: He divides the book around what he calls fake money, fake teachers and fake assets. These labels belong to his argument about currency and financial education and carry his strong personal views.
Fake|Robert T. Kiyosaki.author: Robert Kiyosaki built an education business around Rich Dad Poor Dad. This later book returns to the distrust of conventional financial advice that runs through his work.

Filthy Rich|James Patterson.brief: An account of Jeffrey Epstein's abuse and the institutions that failed his victims.
Filthy Rich|James Patterson.synopsis: Patterson and his coauthors reconstruct the Palm Beach investigation and the favorable treatment Epstein received. The book appeared in 2016, before the later federal arrest brought the case renewed attention.
Filthy Rich|James Patterson.author: Novelist James Patterson wrote this nonfiction account with journalists John Connolly and Tim Malloy. Their reporting grounds a story often told through Epstein's celebrity contacts.

Focus|Daniel Goleman.brief: Goleman examines what happens when attention moves between oneself, other people and the surrounding world.
Focus|Daniel Goleman.synopsis: A leader can read a spreadsheet and still miss the mood of a room. Goleman looks at the distinct kinds of attention involved and how the demands on one can crowd out another.
Focus|Daniel Goleman.author: Daniel Goleman trained in psychology and reported on science for The New York Times. He returned to questions about attention after writing Emotional Intelligence.

Founders at Work|Jessica Livingston.brief: Founders remember the early days before their companies had a success story to tell.
Founders at Work|Jessica Livingston.synopsis: Livingston's interviews linger over half-built products, broken partnerships and the first person willing to pay. Reading the accounts side by side reveals how little the founders could take for granted at the time.
Founders at Work|Jessica Livingston.author: Jessica Livingston co-founded Y Combinator. She interviewed founders herself, giving them room to describe details that had fallen out of the polished versions of their company histories.

Games People Play|Eric Berne.brief: Berne gives names to the recurring exchanges that leave both parties feeling strangely familiar resentment.
Games People Play|Eric Berne.synopsis: He describes social encounters in which the spoken request differs from the reward each person is pursuing. Short cases introduce his vocabulary for these patterns in relationships.
Games People Play|Eric Berne.author: Eric Berne was a psychiatrist who developed transactional analysis. The book brought ideas he used in clinical work to a much wider readership in the 1960s.

Getting Things Done|David Allen.brief: Allen sets up a system for getting unfinished commitments out of your head.
Getting Things Done|David Allen.synopsis: A vague obligation becomes a next physical action, a calendar entry or something to review later. The weekly review keeps that external list credible enough to stop mentally rehearsing it.
Getting Things Done|David Allen.author: David Allen developed the approach while advising executives on managing their work. Its smallest unit is an action someone can actually take, even in the middle of a crowded day.

Goals|Brian Tracy.brief: Tracy works backward from a written goal to the next thing a person can do.
Goals|Brian Tracy.synopsis: The exercises ask readers to set a deadline, name obstacles and specify the skills or help they need. Reviewing the written goal makes it possible to notice when a plan has stopped moving.
Goals|Brian Tracy.author: Brian Tracy taught salespeople and business audiences before writing about personal achievement. The book reads like the written component of one of his practical seminars.

Good to Great|Jim Collins.brief: What changed inside companies whose returns broke away after years of ordinary results?
Good to Great|Jim Collins.synopsis: His team matched these firms with comparison companies and looked for differences in leadership and operations. The cases led to terms such as the hedgehog concept, a way to narrow a company's focus.
Good to Great|Jim Collins.author: Jim Collins led the research after coauthoring Built to Last. The historical selection of companies matters when reading the findings as lessons for a different business.

Gym Launch Secrets|Alex Hormozi.brief: A manual for filling a gym and making its memberships pay for the cost of finding customers.
Gym Launch Secrets|Alex Hormozi.synopsis: Hormozi looks at the offer a prospective member sees, the first sale and what persuades someone to stay. The numbers are those of a local service business with a fixed amount of space.
Gym Launch Secrets|Alex Hormozi.author: Alex Hormozi operated gyms before starting Gym Launch with Leila Hormozi. This book addresses the specific business they helped other owners run.

High Output Management|Andrew S. Grove.brief: Grove measures a manager's work by what the team can produce.
High Output Management|Andrew S. Grove.synopsis: A breakfast order becomes a miniature production line. Grove carries the same reasoning into meetings, one-to-ones and training, where a small amount of managerial time can affect many people's work.
High Output Management|Andrew S. Grove.author: Andrew Grove wrote this while leading operations at Intel. Semiconductor production gave him unusually concrete examples of bottlenecks and of mistakes that become more expensive downstream.

How Asia Works|Joe Studwell.brief: Why did government-backed factories thrive in some East Asian economies and languish in others?
How Asia Works|Joe Studwell.synopsis: Studwell compares land reform, manufacturing policy and the use of bank credit across countries. The test he follows is whether protected firms eventually had to sell goods that could compete abroad.
How Asia Works|Joe Studwell.author: Joe Studwell spent years reporting on Asian economies. The comparative form lets him examine policies that looked similar on paper but produced very different results.

How They Get You|Chris Kohler.brief: Kohler follows the small charges that make an ordinary week more expensive.
How They Get You|Chris Kohler.synopsis: Gift cards, loyalty programs and fees become case studies in how a seller shapes the choices a buyer sees. He asks who makes money when a customer forgets a deadline or leaves a balance unused.
How They Get You|Chris Kohler.author: Chris Kohler is an Australian business journalist. His reporting on household economics supplies the setting for these examples from everyday consumer life.

How to Become Insanely Well-Connected|Fi.brief: Chris Fralic explains what makes someone remember a first conversation years later.
How to Become Insanely Well-Connected|Fi.synopsis: The profile follows the small obligations that come after an introduction. A specific thank-you or a promised piece of work gives the other person a reason to keep the conversation going.
How to Become Insanely Well-Connected|Fi.author: First Round Review interviewed Fralic, a First Round investor with a background in sales. An early encounter with venture capitalist John Doerr helps explain how he learned to follow up.

How to Get Rich|Felix Dennis.brief: A publisher gives a candid account of what getting rich required of him.
How to Get Rich|Felix Dennis.synopsis: Dennis writes about ownership, hiring and the difficult point at which a founder has to cede control of daily work. He also gives an unusually personal reckoning of what his fortune cost him.
How to Get Rich|Felix Dennis.author: Felix Dennis made his money in magazine publishing. He wrote the book after achieving the goal in its title, with enough distance to question parts of the bargain.

How to Make Money in Stocks|William J. O.brief: O'Neil looks for recurring traits in stocks before their largest advances.
How to Make Money in Stocks|William J. O.synopsis: His CAN SLIM method combines earnings growth with price and trading volume. Annotated charts ask readers to inspect what was observable at the time of purchase.
How to Make Money in Stocks|William J. O.author: William O'Neil ran a brokerage and founded Investor's Business Daily. He built a historical database of winning stocks to develop the approach he taught individual investors.

How to Make Shit Happen|Sean Whalen.brief: Whalen asks readers to turn a chaotic week into a small set of daily commitments.
How to Make Shit Happen|Sean Whalen.synopsis: He groups daily work around body, relationships, business and personal reflection. Each area gets an action the reader can point to at the end of the day.
How to Make Shit Happen|Sean Whalen.author: Sean Whalen built the Lions Not Sheep coaching brand. The blunt tone and daily exercises come from the way he addresses his business and self-development audience.

How to Win Friends and Influence People|.brief: Carnegie studies what makes people willing to listen to one another.
How to Win Friends and Influence People|.synopsis: He draws on conversations in sales, management and ordinary social life. Remembering a name or admitting an error matters because it changes what the other person has to defend.
How to Win Friends and Influence People|.author: Dale Carnegie taught public speaking to adults. The book grew from classroom experiments with people who wanted help getting along with colleagues as much as they wanted to give better speeches.

Hyper Learning|Edward D. Hess.brief: Hess asks what people need to keep learning when machines take over more routine work.
Hyper Learning|Edward D. Hess.synopsis: The focus falls on listening, questioning assumptions and creating a workplace where an error can be discussed. He treats learning as behavior people have to practise together.
Hyper Learning|Edward D. Hess.author: Edward Hess taught at the University of Virginia's Darden School of Business after a career in business. He studied how organizations learn and why defensiveness gets in the way.

Hyperfocus: How to Work Less to Achieve.brief: Bailey pairs periods of sustained attention with time for a mind to wander.
Hyperfocus: How to Work Less to Achieve.synopsis: He calls the first mode hyperfocus and the second scatterfocus. One helps finish a chosen task, while the other gives stray thoughts enough room to meet and produce an idea.
Hyperfocus: How to Work Less to Achieve.author: Chris Bailey tested productivity practices on himself and wrote about the results. Here he concentrates on what a person pays attention to once time has already been set aside.

Influence: Psychology of Persuasion|Robe.brief: Why do a favor, a scarce item or a roomful of other buyers change what we agree to?
Influence: Psychology of Persuasion|Robe.synopsis: Cialdini organizes persuasion around recurring social cues. He explains why a shortcut that usually serves a person well can also be used by someone who knows how to trigger it.
Influence: Psychology of Persuasion|Robe.author: Robert Cialdini was a social psychologist at Arizona State University. Alongside experimental research, he spent time among professional persuaders to see how they worked outside the laboratory.

Invent it, Sell it, Bank it|Lori Greiner.brief: Greiner follows a consumer invention from its first sketch to the retail shelf.
Invent it, Sell it, Bank it|Lori Greiner.synopsis: The tasks include checking whether anybody wants the product, negotiating manufacturing and demonstrating it to a buyer. A clever prototype still has to survive its price tag and packaging.
Invent it, Sell it, Bank it|Lori Greiner.author: Lori Greiner built a consumer-products business and sold inventions on QVC. Her advice draws on having to demonstrate a product's use in the time a television viewer was willing to give it.

It Doesn’t Have to Be Crazy at Work|Jaso.brief: Fried and Hansson describe how they run a software company without treating chronic overwork as normal.
It Doesn’t Have to Be Crazy at Work|Jaso.synopsis: They examine meeting policies, deadlines and customer expectations at Basecamp. Each short chapter asks which management decision created a particular demand on employees' time.
It Doesn’t Have to Be Crazy at Work|Jaso.author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson led Basecamp while writing the book. They could try the policies in their own company and describe the tradeoffs they accepted.

James Bond|Ian Fleming.brief: Ian Fleming sends a British intelligence officer into the espionage of the Cold War.
James Bond|Ian Fleming.synopsis: The Bond stories pair assignments with precise details of travel, equipment and physical risk. This shelf entry refers to the series, so a single mission would give a misleading idea of its scope.
James Bond|Ian Fleming.author: Fleming served in British naval intelligence during the Second World War. Afterward he wrote the Bond novels at his home in Jamaica, starting with Casino Royale.

Judgment in Managerial Decision Making|M.brief: A decision-making textbook about the errors managers make even when they have enough information.
Judgment in Managerial Decision Making|M.synopsis: Bazerman and Moore use exercises to let readers make a judgment before seeing the research behind it. Negotiations, forecasts and estimates expose different ways confidence can outrun accuracy.
Judgment in Managerial Decision Making|M.author: Max Bazerman and Don Moore study behavioral decision-making. The book developed through teaching management students who would have to recognize these errors in their own decisions.

Leonardo da Vinci|Walter Isaacson.brief: Isaacson reads Leonardo's notebooks alongside the paintings they helped make possible.
Leonardo da Vinci|Walter Isaacson.synopsis: A marginal question about water or a sketch of a muscle can lead back to a finished picture. The biography also leaves room for commissions Leonardo delayed or never completed.
Leonardo da Vinci|Walter Isaacson.author: Walter Isaacson built this biography around pages that survive in Leonardo's own hand. That choice gave him access to the artist's questions as well as his public achievements.

Let My People Go Surfing|Yvon Chouinard.brief: Patagonia's founder explains what he wanted the company to be able to do differently.
Let My People Go Surfing|Yvon Chouinard.synopsis: Chouinard traces the move from climbing hardware to clothing and the environmental choices that followed. Product design and employment policies become part of the same account of ownership.
Let My People Go Surfing|Yvon Chouinard.author: Yvon Chouinard was a climber and a maker of pitons before becoming a clothing-company founder. He wrote partly to put Patagonia's business philosophy in reach of its employees.

Letters From a Stoic|Seneca.brief: Seneca writes to a friend about how to spend a life whose length nobody can know.
Letters From a Stoic|Seneca.synopsis: Money, illness and the prospect of death recur across the letters. A passing incident often becomes the occasion for a question about what a person actually controls.
Letters From a Stoic|Seneca.author: Seneca wrote the letters to Lucilius late in his life, after serving at Nero's court. Their advice about wealth and public position came from someone who had held both.

Lost and Founder|Rand Fishkin.brief: Fishkin's memoir follows a venture-backed software company through the years when growth stopped feeling simple.
Lost and Founder|Rand Fishkin.synopsis: Moz begins as an SEO business and takes on the expectations that come with outside funding. Fishkin writes about a founder's public optimism alongside the difficult decisions employees rarely see.
Lost and Founder|Rand Fishkin.author: Rand Fishkin co-founded Moz and stepped down as CEO before writing the book. That distance let him revisit financing decisions he had once argued for himself.

Main Street Millionaire|Codie Sanchez.brief: Sanchez looks for existing local businesses whose owners are ready to sell.
Main Street Millionaire|Codie Sanchez.synopsis: She follows the steps between identifying a business and understanding what its cash flow can support. The book gives particular attention to businesses a new owner must operate after the deal closes.
Main Street Millionaire|Codie Sanchez.author: Codie Sanchez worked in finance before buying small businesses. She writes about the less visible part of the acquisition market, where the owner may still answer the telephone.

Makers and Takers|Rana Foroohar.brief: Foroohar asks what happens when making money from financial transactions pays better than making things.
Makers and Takers|Rana Foroohar.synopsis: She follows the growth of financial priorities inside American companies. Decisions about share prices and debt can alter what remains available for factories, workers and research.
Makers and Takers|Rana Foroohar.author: Rana Foroohar reported on business and economics in the years around the financial crisis. The book grew out of her reporting on the relationship between Wall Street and the wider economy.

Mastering the Market Cycle|Howard Marks.brief: Marks asks how an investor can judge where a market stands without predicting its next move.
Mastering the Market Cycle|Howard Marks.synopsis: He follows cycles in credit, profits and investor confidence. A lender's willingness to accept weaker terms can reveal as much about the cycle as the level of a stock index.
Mastering the Market Cycle|Howard Marks.author: Howard Marks co-founded Oaktree Capital Management. His work investing in distressed debt made shifts in credit availability an especially practical concern.

Mastery|Robert Greene.brief: Greene looks at the long apprenticeship behind exceptional work.
Mastery|Robert Greene.synopsis: Historical and contemporary cases follow people through imitation, experimentation and an eventual departure from their teachers. The emphasis falls on the years usually compressed into a sentence in a biography.
Mastery|Robert Greene.author: Robert Greene drew on biographical research and interviews. His own path through a succession of jobs also informed his interest in how people discover what work suits them.

Measure What Matters|John Doerr.brief: Doerr describes how a team can state an objective and tell whether it is getting anywhere.
Measure What Matters|John Doerr.synopsis: Objectives name an intended result, and key results supply observable tests. Examples at Google and elsewhere show how teams use them to negotiate priorities and review missed goals.
Measure What Matters|John Doerr.author: John Doerr learned the approach at Intel under Andy Grove. As a venture investor, he later introduced it to the founders of Google.

Meditations|Marcus Aurelius.brief: A Roman emperor reminds himself how to face an irritating person, a bad day and his own death.
Meditations|Marcus Aurelius.synopsis: Marcus returns to irritation, distraction and the knowledge that his life is short. The repetitions make sense as exercises he needed to do again, even after he knew the argument.
Meditations|Marcus Aurelius.author: Marcus Aurelius kept these notes for himself during his reign. Some passages name places on campaign. Their repetitions make sense in a private notebook. He was rehearsing judgments he would need again tomorrow.

Mind Over Money|Brad Klontz & Ted Klontz.brief: The Klontzes examine the money beliefs people acquire before they are old enough to balance an account.
Mind Over Money|Brad Klontz & Ted Klontz.synopsis: They trace recurring financial behavior back to family experiences and unspoken rules. Exercises ask readers to identify the story behind a decision that otherwise looks irrational.
Mind Over Money|Brad Klontz & Ted Klontz.author: Brad and Ted Klontz are a son and father who worked in financial psychology. Their approach grew out of bringing therapeutic methods to conversations about money.

Mindset: The New Psychology of Success|C.brief: Dweck examines what people do after a mistake when they believe ability can grow.
Mindset: The New Psychology of Success|C.synopsis: Scenes from classrooms, sports and work show how praise and feedback can direct attention toward learning or toward protecting a reputation. Effort matters alongside strategies and opportunities to practise.
Mindset: The New Psychology of Success|C.author: Carol Dweck is a psychologist whose research investigated children's responses to failure. Classroom experiments supplied the distinction she later called fixed and growth mindsets.

Mini Habits|Stephen Guise.brief: Guise builds a habit around a minimum so small it is hard to refuse.
Mini Habits|Stephen Guise.synopsis: One push-up is enough to count. Doing more is allowed, but the tiny requirement stays fixed so getting started never depends on feeling particularly motivated.
Mini Habits|Stephen Guise.author: Stephen Guise developed the idea while trying to make himself exercise. His one-push-up experiment became the example he could explain from personal experience.

Misbehaving|Richard H. Thaler.brief: Thaler tells the story of the economists who took apparently foolish human choices seriously.
Misbehaving|Richard H. Thaler.synopsis: Anomalies such as keeping separate mental accounts for identical dollars become clues to how people decide. Thaler recalls the arguments involved in getting these observations into economic research.
Misbehaving|Richard H. Thaler.author: Richard Thaler helped establish behavioral economics. This is partly a participant's history, including his collaboration with psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky.

Money: Master the Game|Tony Robbins.brief: Robbins interviews investors about what an individual saver can keep after fees and losses.
Money: Master the Game|Tony Robbins.synopsis: The book moves between basic savings decisions and conversations about diversifying a portfolio. Robbins asks professional money managers to explain which ideas an ordinary household might use.
Money: Master the Game|Tony Robbins.author: Tony Robbins came to the subject as a speaker and coach. He undertook the interviews after the financial crisis, when many of his readers had questions about whom to trust with their savings.

Moral Mazes|Robert Jackall.brief: What does a manager learn to call ethical inside a large corporation?
Moral Mazes|Robert Jackall.synopsis: Jackall follows managers through promotions, reversals and decisions whose authorship can become hard to trace. Their working definitions of responsibility shift with the demands of the hierarchy.
Moral Mazes|Robert Jackall.author: Sociologist Robert Jackall conducted fieldwork inside American corporations. Interviews and observation let him study the informal rules that employees seldom put in writing.

More Everything Forever|Adam Becker.brief: Becker investigates the grand futures promised by some of Silicon Valley's most influential thinkers.
More Everything Forever|Adam Becker.synopsis: Space settlements, radical life extension and machine intelligence become questions about resources and power. Becker asks who gets to define the future when a speculative idea attracts substantial funding.
More Everything Forever|Adam Becker.author: Adam Becker trained in astrophysics and writes about science. He approaches these promises by examining both their physical assumptions and the people financing them.

More Money Than Trust|Graham Duncan.brief: Graham Duncan's subject is the trust involved in letting someone else manage money.
More Money Than Trust|Graham Duncan.synopsis: This shelf title has no confirmed publication match. In a related essay, Duncan describes calling references and comparing firsthand accounts to understand the person on the other side of an investment.
More Money Than Trust|Graham Duncan.author: Duncan co-founded East Rock Capital and has written about selecting investment managers. His work puts him on the side of the person deciding whom to entrust with capital.

Nail it Then Scale it|Nathan Furr & Paul.brief: Furr and Ahlstrom ask founders to test the problem before building a company around the answer.
Nail it Then Scale it|Nathan Furr & Paul.synopsis: Customer conversations and small tests precede a larger investment in sales and staff. The book follows the point where learning what customers want gives way to repeating a sale that works.
Nail it Then Scale it|Nathan Furr & Paul.author: Nathan Furr studied entrepreneurship. Paul Ahlstrom brought experience founding and funding companies, where scaling a mistaken assumption could become expensive very quickly.

Never Eat Alone|Keith Ferrazzi & Tahl Ra.brief: Ferrazzi describes the work of keeping in touch before either person needs a favor.
Never Eat Alone|Keith Ferrazzi & Tahl Ra.synopsis: Shared meals, introductions and follow-up make up much of the book. Ferrazzi is especially interested in how someone outside an established circle can begin contributing to it.
Never Eat Alone|Keith Ferrazzi & Tahl Ra.author: Keith Ferrazzi worked in marketing leadership roles at Deloitte and Starwood. He wrote with journalist Tahl Raz about relationships that had shaped his own career.

Never Finished|David Goggins.brief: Goggins returns to what happened after the accomplishments described in his first memoir.
Never Finished|David Goggins.synopsis: Later races and setbacks raise a different problem. Once a difficult goal has been reached, the methods that got a person there may still leave unfinished work. Reflection exercises follow the stories.
Never Finished|David Goggins.author: David Goggins wrote this sequel after his military career and years in endurance events. He could look back on both the public image created by his first book and the work that followed it.

Never Split the Difference|Chris Voss.brief: A former FBI hostage negotiator explains how he got strangers under pressure to keep talking.
Never Split the Difference|Chris Voss.synopsis: Mirroring someone's last words and naming an emotion are ways of hearing more before making an offer. Voss follows actual negotiations and then applies their lessons to less extreme disputes.
Never Split the Difference|Chris Voss.author: Chris Voss negotiated kidnappings for the FBI. He wrote with journalist Tahl Raz after moving into teaching negotiation to business audiences.

Nonviolent Communication|Marshall B. Ros.brief: Rosenberg offers a way to say what hurt without making the other person defend their character.
Nonviolent Communication|Marshall B. Ros.synopsis: He separates an observation from a judgment and a request from a demand. Sample conversations let a reader hear how a small change in wording can alter a difficult exchange.
Nonviolent Communication|Marshall B. Ros.author: Marshall Rosenberg trained as a clinical psychologist and worked as a mediator. His method grew out of trying to keep communication possible across deep disagreement.

Ogilvy on Advertising|David Ogilvy.brief: Ogilvy opens the files on how advertisements get researched, written and judged.
Ogilvy on Advertising|David Ogilvy.synopsis: He annotates actual campaigns and compares the demands of print, television and direct mail. The examples show how much information he expected an advertisement to carry.
Ogilvy on Advertising|David Ogilvy.author: David Ogilvy wrote this later book after decades running an advertising agency. He could revisit campaigns with both their creative decisions and commercial results in view.

One Up On Wall Street|Peter Lynch.brief: Lynch asks when noticing a good business gives an ordinary investor a place to start researching.
One Up On Wall Street|Peter Lynch.synopsis: A crowded store or a product people buy repeatedly can be a lead. Lynch then works through the accounts and company type to see whether the stock price already assumes that success.
One Up On Wall Street|Peter Lynch.author: Peter Lynch managed Fidelity's Magellan Fund. He wrote with John Rothchild while his experience selecting companies was still part of his daily work.

One to Many|Jason Fladlien.brief: Fladlien treats a webinar as a sales conversation with many listeners at once.
One to Many|Jason Fladlien.synopsis: He works backward from the offer to the questions a presentation needs to answer. Timing, examples and the transition to a purchase all get attention.
One to Many|Jason Fladlien.author: Jason Fladlien built a business selling and teaching through webinars. He wrote for presenters who have to hold an audience long enough to explain an unfamiliar offer.

Open|Andre Agassi.brief: Andre Agassi could hit a tennis ball for hours before he was old enough to choose the game.
Open|Andre Agassi.synopsis: His father's ball machine, years on tour and a hard-won return to competition give the memoir its shape. Private ambivalence runs through some of its most public victories.
Open|Andre Agassi.author: Andre Agassi wrote after retiring from professional tennis. He worked closely with writer J. R. Moehringer to reconstruct the experiences behind the scores.

Other People’s Money|John Kay.brief: Kay asks which parts of modern finance actually serve households and businesses.
Other People’s Money|John Kay.synopsis: He starts with the purposes of finance, such as payments and funding investment, then examines a system increasingly occupied with trading existing claims. The distance between a saver and an end borrower is central.
Other People’s Money|John Kay.author: British economist John Kay reviewed equity markets for the UK government after the financial crisis. That work informed his interest in the chain of intermediaries handling other people's money.

Outliers|Malcolm Gladwell.brief: Gladwell examines the opportunities hidden inside stories of individual success.
Outliers|Malcolm Gladwell.synopsis: Birth dates in youth hockey and early access to computers complicate the idea that talent explains an outcome by itself. The cases ask who got the practice, timing and access that others missed.
Outliers|Malcolm Gladwell.author: Malcolm Gladwell was a staff writer at The New Yorker. He used reported stories to bring research about achievement and opportunity to a general audience.

Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevit.brief: Attia asks what it would take to stay capable in the last decades of life.
Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevit.synopsis: The book organizes preventive care around major chronic diseases and the physical abilities a person hopes to retain. Attia discusses exercise and metabolic health through the priorities of his clinical practice.
Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevit.author: Peter Attia trained in surgery and later built a practice focused on longevity. He wrote the book with journalist Bill Gifford to explain the reasoning behind that practice.

Pitch Anything|Oren Klaff.brief: Klaff studies what happens before the facts in a pitch get a fair hearing.
Pitch Anything|Oren Klaff.synopsis: He pays attention to who defines the meeting and how a listener decides what deserves attention. His examples come from presentations where securing the next conversation mattered as much as the slide deck.
Pitch Anything|Oren Klaff.author: Oren Klaff worked in investment banking and capital raising. The book grows out of pitching deals to people who routinely hear more proposals than they can consider.

Pivot|Jenny Blake.brief: Blake treats a career change as a series of small trials.
Pivot|Jenny Blake.synopsis: Start with skills and relationships that already exist, then test possible directions before making a larger move. A short project can answer questions a job description leaves open.
Pivot|Jenny Blake.author: Jenny Blake worked in career development at Google before leaving to work independently. She drew on that transition and on conversations with people facing similar decisions.

Poor Charlie's Almanack|Charles T. Munge.brief: Charlie Munger borrows from psychology and probability to explain why smart people make expensive mistakes.
Poor Charlie's Almanack|Charles T. Munge.synopsis: The collection mixes speeches with biographical material and commentary. Munger returns to the ways incentives and several ordinary biases can combine to produce an extraordinary mistake.
Poor Charlie's Almanack|Charles T. Munge.author: Munger spent decades making investment decisions alongside Warren Buffett at Berkshire Hathaway. Peter Kaufman edited these talks, keeping the jokes and digressions that made Munger sound like himself.

Pre-Suasion: A Revolutionary Way to Infl.brief: Cialdini studies the moment before somebody hears a request.
Pre-Suasion: A Revolutionary Way to Infl.synopsis: A question or an image can steer attention toward one consideration before a proposal is even made. The book examines experiments in which changing that first moment changed the response that followed.
Pre-Suasion: A Revolutionary Way to Infl.author: Social psychologist Robert Cialdini returned to persuasion after years of studying what makes a message effective. This time he asked what a communicator does before delivering it.

Predictable Revenue|Aaron Ross & Marylou.brief: Ross and Tyler separate the job of finding a prospect from the job of closing the sale.
Predictable Revenue|Aaron Ross & Marylou.synopsis: They describe a sales organization with distinct roles and a repeatable way to start conversations. The examples show why expecting one representative to do every part can make revenue hard to forecast.
Predictable Revenue|Aaron Ross & Marylou.author: Aaron Ross developed an outbound sales team at Salesforce. Marylou Tyler brought experience in sales development and process design to their account of how the model works.

Principles|Ray Dalio.brief: Dalio sets out the rules he wrote for making decisions and running Bridgewater.
Principles|Ray Dalio.synopsis: Personal mistakes become rules to consult when a similar situation recurs. In the workplace sections he describes how employees challenge each other and how the firm weighs disagreement.
Principles|Ray Dalio.author: Ray Dalio founded Bridgewater Associates. The work began as principles circulated inside the investment firm before he expanded them into a book for the public.

Problem Solving 101|Ken Watanabe.brief: A children's rock band gives Watanabe a way to teach problem solving with pencil and paper.
Problem Solving 101|Ken Watanabe.synopsis: Simple cases ask readers to define a problem, sort possible causes and decide what evidence would distinguish them. Diagrams make each step visible enough for someone else to challenge it.
Problem Solving 101|Ken Watanabe.author: Ken Watanabe worked at McKinsey and originally wrote the book for young readers in Japan. That original audience accounts for its small cases and accessible diagrams.

Psycho-Cybernetics|Maxwell Maltz.brief: Maltz asks why a change in appearance does not always change the way a person sees themselves.
Psycho-Cybernetics|Maxwell Maltz.synopsis: He compares self-image to an internal guidance system and proposes rehearsal and imagery exercises. His case material begins with patients whose confidence did or did not change after surgery.
Psycho-Cybernetics|Maxwell Maltz.author: Maxwell Maltz was a plastic surgeon. The mismatch he observed between a successful operation and a patient's sense of self prompted him to write beyond the boundaries of his specialty.

Reach Out, Stay in Touch and Deepen Your.brief: Practical advice on what to say between a first introduction and the next time you meet.
Reach Out, Stay in Touch and Deepen Your.synopsis: First Round collects ways to make an introduction specific, follow up with something useful and reach out after a long silence. The focus is the awkward middle of a relationship, after names have been exchanged.
Reach Out, Stay in Touch and Deepen Your.author: First Round Review drew the piece from interviews with operators and investors in its archive. The result brings several practitioners' habits together rather than attributing one method to a single author.

Read People Like a Book|Patrick King.brief: King asks what you can reasonably infer about someone from what they say and do.
Read People Like a Book|Patrick King.synopsis: He considers motives, body language and repeated behavior. His examples encourage looking at context and patterns before drawing conclusions from one expression or gesture.
Read People Like a Book|Patrick King.author: Patrick King writes and coaches on social skills. He frames observation as a skill readers can practise in everyday conversations.

Read Write Own|Chris Dixon.brief: Dixon describes internet networks that give participants a claim on the systems they use.
Read Write Own|Chris Dixon.synopsis: The argument follows a shift from open protocols to platforms owned by companies. Dixon presents blockchains as a possible ownership model and examines the economic incentives behind that proposal.
Read Write Own|Chris Dixon.author: Chris Dixon founded technology companies before leading crypto investing at Andreessen Horowitz. He writes as an investor with a stated interest in the networks he describes.

Ready, Fire, Aim|Michael Masterson.brief: Masterson divides a growing company's problems by its stage of revenue.
Ready, Fire, Aim|Michael Masterson.synopsis: Early chapters concentrate on making the first dependable sales. Later ones turn to hiring and management, when a founder can become the constraint on a business that already knows how to sell.
Ready, Fire, Aim|Michael Masterson.author: Michael Masterson is a pen name of entrepreneur and direct-response marketer Mark Ford. He drew on businesses he helped build in publishing and related fields.

Reality Transurfing|Vadim Zeland.brief: Zeland imagines life as a set of possible paths a person can learn to navigate.
Reality Transurfing|Vadim Zeland.synopsis: The books develop a vocabulary of alternative realities and forces he calls pendulums. Within this metaphysical system, reducing the importance assigned to an outcome is one way to change a person's relationship to it.
Reality Transurfing|Vadim Zeland.author: Vadim Zeland is the author associated with the Russian Transurfing series. Reliable biographical detail is scarce, and the system is best read on its own stated metaphysical terms.

Relentless|Tim S. Grover.brief: Grover describes what elite basketball players ask of themselves after ordinary training ends.
Relentless|Tim S. Grover.synopsis: He sorts competitors by how they respond to pressure and examines the habits of players who demand the ball when an outcome is uncertain. The portraits draw on time spent in training rooms.
Relentless|Tim S. Grover.author: Tim Grover trained Michael Jordan and other professional athletes. He wrote with Shari Wenk about the mental demands he saw alongside physical preparation.

Rework|Jason Fried & David Heinemeier Ha.brief: Two software founders question the meeting, the hiring plan and the product nobody has asked for yet.
Rework|Jason Fried & David Heinemeier Ha.synopsis: Fried and Hansson favor releasing a smaller product and learning from people who actually use it. The essays return to how easily a growing company can spend time coordinating work that nobody needs.
Rework|Jason Fried & David Heinemeier Ha.author: The authors ran 37signals, the software company behind Basecamp. They wrote while building products with a small team and financing the business through customers.

Rich Dad Poor Dad|Robert T. Kiyosaki.brief: Kiyosaki contrasts two approaches to earning money through the figures of two fathers.
Rich Dad Poor Dad|Robert T. Kiyosaki.synopsis: He uses household balance sheets and stories about work to explain why he prizes ownership and cash flow. The two fathers function as teachers in his account of learning about money.
Rich Dad Poor Dad|Robert T. Kiyosaki.author: Robert Kiyosaki built his career around financial education. The book's first-person teaching stories established the format he later used throughout the Rich Dad series.

Rich Dad’s Guide to Investing|Robert T..brief: Kiyosaki asks what changes when an investor can build or buy a business.
Rich Dad’s Guide to Investing|Robert T..synopsis: The book distinguishes kinds of investors and the preparation he thinks each needs. Much of the discussion turns on who controls an asset and how to read the cash flowing through it.
Rich Dad’s Guide to Investing|Robert T..author: Robert Kiyosaki wrote this as part of his Rich Dad series with Sharon Lechter. It develops the investing side of the earlier book's argument for financial education.

Rich Kid Smart Kid|Robert T. Kiyosaki.brief: How might a family teach a child about money before the child's first paycheck?
Rich Kid Smart Kid|Robert T. Kiyosaki.synopsis: Kiyosaki connects conversations at home with games and examples meant to make financial choices visible. He questions how well conventional schooling prepares children to evaluate those choices.
Rich Kid Smart Kid|Robert T. Kiyosaki.author: Robert Kiyosaki and Sharon Lechter developed educational materials around money. This entry in their Rich Dad series turns to the adults responsible for teaching children.

Richsterious Autopilot Money|Richsterius.brief: An independently marketed ebook about earning money on autopilot.
Richsterious Autopilot Money|Richsterius.synopsis: Richsterius sells this title alongside Money Slave as part of its financial-freedom collection. The public listing identifies the work but gives little detail about the specific methods it contains.
Richsterious Autopilot Money|Richsterius.author: Richsterius is the publishing name on the cover and storefront. The publisher provides no named individual author or professional biography there.

Right Thing, Right Now|Ryan Holiday.brief: Holiday asks what acting justly requires when doing so costs the person making the choice.
Right Thing, Right Now|Ryan Holiday.synopsis: His historical cases turn on obligations to strangers, colleagues and opponents. Keeping a promise becomes more revealing when nobody can compel a person to honor it.
Right Thing, Right Now|Ryan Holiday.author: Ryan Holiday wrote this as the justice volume in his series on the classical virtues. It follows his books on courage and temperance.

Rising Strong|Brené Brown.brief: Brown looks at the story people tell themselves immediately after something painful happens.
Rising Strong|Brené Brown.synopsis: She follows the movement from an initial interpretation to a more careful account of what happened. The examples give particular attention to shame and the temptation to protect oneself by assigning blame.
Rising Strong|Brené Brown.author: Brené Brown trained as a social worker and researched vulnerability and shame. She wrote this after readers of her earlier work began asking what to do after taking a risk went badly.

Sapiens|Yuval Noah Harari.brief: Harari tells a history of humanity through changes in what large groups can believe and do together.
Sapiens|Yuval Noah Harari.synopsis: He moves through agriculture, empires and scientific inquiry, asking how shared stories and institutions make cooperation possible among strangers. The scale is the species rather than a particular nation.
Sapiens|Yuval Noah Harari.author: Yuval Noah Harari taught history at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. The book grew out of a broad survey course that asked students to connect events normally studied in isolation.

Secrets of the Millionaire Mind|T. Harv.brief: Eker asks readers to examine the financial expectations they inherited at home.
Secrets of the Millionaire Mind|T. Harv.synopsis: His idea of a money blueprint links early messages about wealth with later habits of earning, spending and saving. The exercises invite readers to identify those messages in their own histories.
Secrets of the Millionaire Mind|T. Harv.author: T. Harv Eker taught money seminars before publishing this book. Its declarations and self-assessments reflect the participatory format of those events.

Sell or Be Sold|Grant Cardone.brief: Cardone treats selling as the work of getting another person to commit to a decision.
Sell or Be Sold|Grant Cardone.synopsis: He considers conviction in a product, follow-up and the discomfort of asking directly for a sale. Examples extend the term selling well beyond a conventional sales job.
Sell or Be Sold|Grant Cardone.author: Grant Cardone trained sales teams, including automobile dealers. His approach is rooted in retail environments where objections and decisions happen face to face.

Shoe Dog|Phil Knight.brief: Before Nike had a name, Phil Knight was selling Japanese running shoes from the trunk of his car.
Shoe Dog|Phil Knight.synopsis: At Blue Ribbon Sports, selling out of shoes could leave Knight too broke to order more. He recalls the runners who joined him, the banker who doubted him and the Japanese supplier whose shoes they would eventually have to replace.
Shoe Dog|Phil Knight.author: Knight ran track at Oregon under Bill Bowerman, who became his business partner. He wrote the memoir decades later, choosing to spend most of it in the years before Nike went public.
