Skin in the Game|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.brief: Taleb asks who bears the loss when somebody else's advice turns out badly.
Skin in the Game|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.synopsis: His examples include traders, officials and professionals insulated from the effects of their decisions. Personal exposure to a downside becomes a test he applies to both fairness and expertise.
Skin in the Game|Nassim Nicholas Taleb.author: Nassim Nicholas Taleb worked as a derivatives trader. This book extends his writing on uncertainty to the incentives of the people who claim they can manage it.

Startup Rising|Christopher Schröder.brief: Schroeder reports on entrepreneurs building technology companies across the Middle East.
Startup Rising|Christopher Schröder.synopsis: Founders describe reaching customers, raising capital and working around patchy infrastructure. The book captures a particular moment when mobile connectivity and political upheaval were changing the region.
Startup Rising|Christopher Schröder.author: Christopher Schroeder is an entrepreneur and investor. Visits to regional startup gatherings led him to spend more time with founders whose companies rarely appeared in American coverage.

Startups for Students|YC Startup Library.brief: A student's guide to choosing between starting a company and joining one.
Startups for Students|YC Startup Library.synopsis: YC collects the questions students kept asking about cofounders, timing and getting experience at a startup. Short answers lead into firsthand accounts and earlier talks in its library.
Startups for Students|YC Startup Library.author: Tamanna Khemani and Kat Mañalac assembled the guide after Y Combinator's virtual outreach tours. They had met thousands of students and could see which questions kept recurring.

Status Anxiety|Alain de Botton.brief: De Botton asks why a change in social standing can feel like a judgment on a whole life.
Status Anxiety|Alain de Botton.synopsis: He traces the wish for recognition through class, work and ideas about merit. Philosophy and art offer other ways of judging a life when the surrounding society equates success with income.
Status Anxiety|Alain de Botton.author: Alain de Botton writes philosophical essays for general readers. Here he uses literature, paintings and social history to examine a worry more often treated as a private failing.

Stories That Stick|Kindra Hall.brief: Hall shows how to find the particular moment that makes a business story worth telling.
Stories That Stick|Kindra Hall.synopsis: She distinguishes stories about a product's value, a founder, a purpose and a customer. The practical work lies in choosing a scene a listener can picture and understanding whose decision it might affect.
Stories That Stick|Kindra Hall.author: Kindra Hall worked as a storyteller and speaker before writing for business audiences. Her examples come from the kinds of presentations in which a polished claim often fails to stick.

Surrounded By Idiots|Thomas Erikson.brief: Erikson uses four colors to discuss the different ways people communicate at work.
Surrounded By Idiots|Thomas Erikson.synopsis: The book walks through fictionalized encounters in which a person's pace or directness gets misread. The colors are a shorthand in the author's communication model, not a clinical assessment.
Surrounded By Idiots|Thomas Erikson.author: Thomas Erikson is a Swedish writer and lecturer on communication. Everyday misunderstandings gave him the premise for a book intended for use outside a psychology classroom.

Tax-Free Wealth|Tom Wheelwright.brief: Wheelwright reads tax rules as clues to the activities governments want to encourage.
Tax-Free Wealth|Tom Wheelwright.synopsis: He uses business and investment examples to show how choices about ownership and expenses can affect tax treatment. The examples reflect the jurisdictions and rules in the edition being read.
Tax-Free Wealth|Tom Wheelwright.author: Tom Wheelwright is a certified public accountant who advises entrepreneurs and investors. He wrote to explain the reasoning he uses in conversations with business owners.

The $100 Startup|Chris Guillebeau.brief: Guillebeau profiles people who found paying customers with very little startup capital.
The $100 Startup|Chris Guillebeau.synopsis: A skill that seems ordinary to its owner can solve a problem for someone else. The cases follow the first offer, the first sale and the costs involved in keeping a small business running.
The $100 Startup|Chris Guillebeau.author: Chris Guillebeau ran independent ventures and wrote about earning a living outside conventional employment. He collected stories from other owners to see how their beginnings differed.

The 10x Rule|Grant Cardone.brief: Cardone argues that people underestimate both the size of a goal and the work it will require.
The 10x Rule|Grant Cardone.synopsis: He lays out levels of action and asks readers to compare their daily activity with the results they expect. Sales prospecting supplies a particularly visible example of the gap.
The 10x Rule|Grant Cardone.author: Grant Cardone built a business training sales organizations. His multiplier reflects the language of targets and activity levels he used with those teams.

The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership|Jo.brief: Maxwell organizes his approach to leadership around twenty-one recurring principles.
The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership|Jo.synopsis: Each chapter studies a different problem, such as earning trust or preparing a successor. Stories give readers a way to connect a principle with a decision they might face.
The 21 Irrefutable Laws of Leadership|Jo.author: John Maxwell led churches before teaching leadership to business and nonprofit audiences. His experience depended heavily on persuading people to participate voluntarily.

The 4 Hour Work Week|Timothy Ferriss.brief: Ferriss takes apart his working week to see which parts still need him there.
The 4 Hour Work Week|Timothy Ferriss.synopsis: Outsourcing routine decisions and testing a small product business are part of a larger experiment in controlling one's time. The travel sections ask what that freedom would actually be used for.
The 4 Hour Work Week|Timothy Ferriss.author: Tim Ferriss was running a sports-nutrition business when he began experimenting with remote management. The book grew out of his effort to travel while the company continued operating.

The 5 Types of Wealth|Sahil Bloom.brief: Bloom asks what a person might accumulate besides money and what earning money can quietly cost.
The 5 Types of Wealth|Sahil Bloom.synopsis: He considers time, relationships, mental life, health and finances as separate forms of wealth. Questions and exercises let readers examine which tradeoffs they are making in a particular season of life.
The 5 Types of Wealth|Sahil Bloom.author: Sahil Bloom worked in finance and wrote a widely read newsletter before publishing the book. His reflections on time with family give the framework a personal starting point.

The 80/20 Principle|Richard Koch.brief: Koch looks for situations where a small share of the causes accounts for most of the result.
The 80/20 Principle|Richard Koch.synopsis: A few customers or products may produce a disproportionate share of profits. Koch uses this unevenness to ask where managers and individuals can stop spending effort.
The 80/20 Principle|Richard Koch.author: Richard Koch worked as a management consultant and investor. He adapted an observation associated with economist Vilfredo Pareto into a practical guide to allocating time and resources.

The Alchemist|Paulo Coelho.brief: An Andalusian shepherd leaves his flock to follow a recurring dream about treasure.
The Alchemist|Paulo Coelho.synopsis: Santiago's journey takes him across the desert, where work, love and chance encounters complicate the promise that first set him moving. Coelho tells it as a fable and leaves its discovery to the reader.
The Alchemist|Paulo Coelho.author: Paulo Coelho was a Brazilian songwriter before turning to novels. He published the book in Portuguese in 1988, after a pilgrimage that also informed his early writing.

The Algebra of Wealth|Scott Galloway.brief: Galloway asks which early choices give a person more control over their financial future.
The Algebra of Wealth|Scott Galloway.synopsis: Career focus, spending habits and long holding periods carry more weight in his account than picking a spectacular investment. He connects financial decisions with where and how a person chooses to work.
The Algebra of Wealth|Scott Galloway.author: Scott Galloway founded businesses and taught marketing at NYU Stern. He draws on both successful ventures and costly mistakes in discussing what founders and employees can realistically control.

The Algorithm|John McNeill.brief: McNeill lays out the five-step operating method he learned at Tesla.
The Algorithm|John McNeill.synopsis: The sequence begins by questioning requirements and deleting unnecessary steps. Simplifying, speeding up and automating come later, since automation can make an unnecessary process expensive to undo.
The Algorithm|John McNeill.author: Jon McNeill led global sales and service at Tesla and later served as Lyft's chief operating officer. He writes about using the method both inside Tesla and after leaving.

The Almanack of Naval Ravikant|Eric Jorg.brief: A collection of Naval Ravikant's remarks on building wealth and living with one's own decisions.
The Almanack of Naval Ravikant|Eric Jorg.synopsis: Short excerpts on ownership, judgment and happiness sit alongside longer passages. The arrangement lets a reader follow one subject across conversations that originally took place years apart.
The Almanack of Naval Ravikant|Eric Jorg.author: Eric Jorgenson selected and organized material from Ravikant's interviews and public writing. The result is an edited reader rather than a continuous memoir written by Ravikant.

The Art of Seduction|Robert Greene.brief: Greene reads historical seductions as exercises in attention, anticipation and power.
The Art of Seduction|Robert Greene.synopsis: He arranges episodes around recurring roles and tactics, with examples drawn from politics as well as romance. His interest lies in how one person can shape another's perception over time.
The Art of Seduction|Robert Greene.author: Robert Greene had previously used court histories to write about power. He returned to several of the same kinds of sources to study influence in more intimate settings.

The Bezos Letters|Steve Anderson.brief: Anderson reads Amazon's shareholder letters as a record of how the company approached growth.
The Bezos Letters|Steve Anderson.synopsis: He draws business principles from the decisions Jeff Bezos explained to shareholders. Long time horizons and a willingness to fund experiments recur even as the business itself changes.
The Bezos Letters|Steve Anderson.author: Steve Anderson studied technology and risk in business. He wrote with Karen Anderson using the public letters, an outsider's source distinct from interviews inside Amazon.

The Book of Five Rings|Miyamoto Musashi.brief: A swordsman's account of timing, distance and the ability to see what an opponent is doing.
The Book of Five Rings|Miyamoto Musashi.synopsis: Musashi places individual combat beside broader questions of strategy. His writing keeps returning to practice, because a useful instruction on the page still has to become a movement.
The Book of Five Rings|Miyamoto Musashi.author: Miyamoto Musashi was a Japanese swordsman who wrote the treatise late in life. He drew on a martial tradition in which a mistaken reading of distance had immediate consequences.

The Boron Letters|Gary C. Halbert.brief: A copywriter in prison writes to his son about sales letters and the life around them.
The Boron Letters|Gary C. Halbert.synopsis: Halbert explains lists, offers and the discipline of studying mail that produces orders. Advice about exercise and daily habits sits beside the advertising lessons because these were letters home.
The Boron Letters|Gary C. Halbert.author: Gary Halbert wrote the letters to his son Bond while incarcerated at Boron Federal Prison Camp. Their informal address and occasional digressions come directly from that circumstance.

The Circadian Code|Satchin Panda.brief: Panda asks what meal times and light exposure have to do with the body's daily clocks.
The Circadian Code|Satchin Panda.synopsis: He follows the rhythms that govern sleep, metabolism and activity. His account of time-restricted eating grew out of laboratory work on when animals ate as well as what they ate.
The Circadian Code|Satchin Panda.author: Satchin Panda researches circadian biology at the Salk Institute. He wrote the book to connect work on cellular clocks with the timing of ordinary daily routines.

The Courage to be Disliked|Ichiro Kishim.brief: A young man and a philosopher argue over whether a person's past determines their future.
The Courage to be Disliked|Ichiro Kishim.synopsis: Over a series of evenings, the philosopher introduces Alfred Adler's ideas about responsibility and the desire for approval. The young man's objections give the argument room to develop.
The Courage to be Disliked|Ichiro Kishim.author: Ichiro Kishimi studied Adlerian psychology. Writer Fumitake Koga worked with him to present those ideas through dialogue, a form that lets the reader follow the questions as well as the answers.

The Daily Laws|Robert Greene.brief: A short reading for each day of the year, drawn from Greene's work on ambition, power and human nature.
The Daily Laws|Robert Greene.synopsis: Each day pairs an observation with a prompt. Monthly themes hold the sequence together, letting readers revisit an idea in small portions rather than reading a historical case in one sitting.
The Daily Laws|Robert Greene.author: Robert Greene assembled the book after writing several longer works on power and mastery. It draws from those books and from the advice readers asked him for afterward.

The E-Myth Revisited|Michael E. Gerber.brief: Gerber explains why being good at a trade can be poor preparation for owning the business that sells it.
The E-Myth Revisited|Michael E. Gerber.synopsis: A fictional pie-shop owner faces the difference between baking a good pie and running a shop that can do so repeatedly. The story introduces documented processes and a clearer division of responsibilities.
The E-Myth Revisited|Michael E. Gerber.author: Michael Gerber worked with small-business owners. He expanded his original E-Myth book around a problem he saw often, an owner's skill becoming the very thing the firm could never operate without.

The Everything Store|Brad Stone.brief: Stone follows Amazon as an online bookseller becomes a retailer with ambitions far beyond books.
The Everything Store|Brad Stone.synopsis: Employees and rivals describe the company's expansion into new categories and services. Stone traces how internal practices formed while the business was changing faster than its competitors expected.
The Everything Store|Brad Stone.author: Brad Stone covered the technology industry as a reporter and interviewed people across Amazon's history. His book appeared before several later chapters in the company's growth.

The Goal|Eliyahu M. Goldratt.brief: A factory keeps every machine busy and still can't ship its orders on time.
The Goal|Eliyahu M. Goldratt.synopsis: Orders are late even though every department is trying to stay busy. Through a series of questions, Alex Rogo learns why improving one machine may do nothing for the plant as a whole.
The Goal|Eliyahu M. Goldratt.author: Eliyahu Goldratt developed the theory of constraints. He wrote the novel with Jeff Cox so readers could reason through the plant's problems before being handed a management rule.

The Greatest Salesman in the World|Og Ma.brief: A young camel boy learns the craft of selling through a set of scrolls.
The Greatest Salesman in the World|Og Ma.synopsis: Mandino builds a fable around repeated readings and the habits they are meant to cultivate. The story treats a salesperson's conduct toward other people as part of the work of selling.
The Greatest Salesman in the World|Og Ma.author: Og Mandino worked in sales and later edited Success Unlimited. He chose a historical fable to present ideas that his original audience usually heard in a sales meeting.

The Hard Thing About Hard Things|Ben Hor.brief: Horowitz writes about the decisions a chief executive still has to make when every option looks bad.
The Hard Thing About Hard Things|Ben Hor.synopsis: Layoffs, replacing executives and keeping a struggling company alive get more space than founding-day optimism. Horowitz revisits decisions he made with incomplete information and employees depending on him.
The Hard Thing About Hard Things|Ben Hor.author: Ben Horowitz led Loudcloud through a difficult transition into the software company Opsware. He later co-founded Andreessen Horowitz, where founders brought him many of the same problems.

The House of Morgan|Ron Chernow.brief: Chernow traces the Morgan banking houses through a century and a half of financial and political change.
The House of Morgan|Ron Chernow.synopsis: Bankers arrange loans for states, intervene in panics and eventually encounter governments powerful enough to curb them. The family story runs alongside a history of how banking authority moved between institutions.
The House of Morgan|Ron Chernow.author: Ron Chernow worked as a journalist before writing this financial history. Archival research let him follow the people and institutions well beyond the lifetime of J. P. Morgan himself.

The Innovator’s Dilemma|Clayton M. Chris.brief: Christensen asks why a well-run company can listen to its best customers and still lose its market.
The Innovator’s Dilemma|Clayton M. Chris.synopsis: The disk-drive industry supplies his central puzzle. A smaller drive can initially look inferior to established buyers while being useful enough for a different market where it has time to improve.
The Innovator’s Dilemma|Clayton M. Chris.author: Clayton Christensen developed the argument through doctoral research at Harvard Business School after working in industry. He wanted to explain patterns of failure that poor management alone could not account for.

The Intelligent Investor|Benjamin Graham.brief: Graham sets out how an investor can allow room for being wrong about a business.
The Intelligent Investor|Benjamin Graham.synopsis: He distinguishes investment from speculation and develops the idea of a margin of safety. His imaginary business partner Mr. Market illustrates why a quoted price and a business's value need not coincide.
The Intelligent Investor|Benjamin Graham.author: Benjamin Graham managed investments and taught security analysis at Columbia. He published the first edition in 1949 after living through a market crash and a long depression.

The Kaisen Challenge|Sarah Harvey.brief: Harvey applies the Japanese idea of continuous improvement to small changes in everyday routines.
The Kaisen Challenge|Sarah Harvey.synopsis: She asks readers to choose a manageable change and observe what happens before extending it. The scale is domestic and personal, rather than the factory floor where many readers first encounter kaizen.
The Kaisen Challenge|Sarah Harvey.author: Sarah Harvey explored Japanese approaches to daily life while living in Tokyo. Her published work on kaizen supplies the context for the spelling used in this shelf entry.

The Lean Startup|Eric Ries.brief: Ries treats a startup's first product as a way to test what its founders believe.
The Lean Startup|Eric Ries.synopsis: A small release can reveal whether customers want the proposed outcome before the team commits to building everything. Ries looks for measures that can distinguish genuine learning from mere activity.
The Lean Startup|Eric Ries.author: Eric Ries co-founded IMVU and drew on its early experiments. He developed the book while bringing ideas from lean manufacturing into conversations among software founders.

The Little Book That Beats the Market|Jo.brief: Greenblatt offers a simple screen for finding profitable companies at relatively low prices.
The Little Book That Beats the Market|Jo.synopsis: The method ranks businesses on measures of earnings yield and return on capital. The book asks why a rule that sounds simple might still be difficult for an investor to follow through lean years.
The Little Book That Beats the Market|Jo.author: Joel Greenblatt ran Gotham Capital and taught investing at Columbia. He wrote the explanation in language intended to be accessible even to his children.

The Lords of Easy Money|Christopher Leon.brief: Leonard follows the Federal Reserve's experiment with exceptionally loose monetary policy.
The Lords of Easy Money|Christopher Leon.synopsis: Through officials, financiers and companies that borrowed in this period, he examines how cheap money affected asset prices and risk-taking. Dissent inside the Fed provides a recurring point of view.
The Lords of Easy Money|Christopher Leon.author: Christopher Leonard is a business journalist. His reporting uses interviews and the experiences of firms outside Washington to trace decisions that otherwise appear mainly as changes in interest rates.

The Millionaire Fastlane|MJ DeMarco.brief: DeMarco asks how the economics of owning a scalable business differ from being paid for hours worked.
The Millionaire Fastlane|MJ DeMarco.synopsis: He divides approaches to wealth into road metaphors, then examines ownership, customer need and scale. His running example is a company whose reach could grow beyond the founder's working day.
The Millionaire Fastlane|MJ DeMarco.author: MJ DeMarco built and sold Limos.com. His frustration with waiting decades for financial independence supplied the premise for the comparison.

The Millionaire Next Door|Thomas J. Stan.brief: Stanley and Danko look at the spending habits of American households that quietly accumulated wealth.
The Millionaire Next Door|Thomas J. Stan.synopsis: They compare outward signs of affluence with net worth and document the budgeting and career choices of their respondents. Many of the households they studied would be easy to miss by appearance alone.
The Millionaire Next Door|Thomas J. Stan.author: Thomas Stanley and William Danko researched affluent consumers. Interviews and surveys undertaken for that work yielded a portrait different from the image many advertisers had of a millionaire.

The Mind of Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte,.brief: Napoleon's remarks on government, warfare and human character, gathered by subject.
The Mind of Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte,.synopsis: The arrangement puts observations made at different times beside one another. It lets a reader compare the general's account of leadership with the emperor's judgments about law, ambition and public opinion.
The Mind of Napoleon|Napoleon Bonaparte,.author: Historian J. Christopher Herold selected and translated Napoleon's words. The organization and selection are Herold's editorial work rather than a treatise Napoleon composed in this form.

The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari|Robin Shar.brief: A lawyer who collapses in court gives up his possessions and leaves to reconsider his life.
The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari|Robin Shar.synopsis: Julian Mantle returns with a set of lessons he learned on his travels. Sharma uses the exchange between Julian and a former colleague to discuss attention, discipline and what professional success can cost.
The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari|Robin Shar.author: Robin Sharma trained as a lawyer before writing about leadership and personal development. A lawyer's crisis gave him a setting whose professional rewards he knew firsthand.

The Motive|Patrick Lencioni.brief: Lencioni asks a chief executive why he wanted the job in the first place.
The Motive|Patrick Lencioni.synopsis: A conversation between two executives exposes the parts of leadership one has been avoiding. The book then looks at difficult conversations and meetings as duties that come with authority.
The Motive|Patrick Lencioni.author: Patrick Lencioni advised leadership teams and used business fables in his teaching. Here he directs the question at the person at the top, whose reasons for leading affect everyone else's work.

The Now Habit|Neil Fiore.brief: Fiore looks at why an important task can become harder to start the longer it waits.
The Now Habit|Neil Fiore.synopsis: His Unschedule places recreation and fixed commitments on the calendar first. The reader then records completed work, shifting attention to short starts and observable progress.
The Now Habit|Neil Fiore.author: Neil Fiore was a psychologist who worked on stress and procrastination. The book treats avoidance as something to understand and plan around rather than a simple shortage of willpower.

The ONE Thing|Gary Keller & Jay Papasan.brief: Keller and Papasan ask which single action would make the rest of a day's work easier.
The ONE Thing|Gary Keller & Jay Papasan.synopsis: They apply a focusing question to long-term goals and the next available block of time. Protecting that block becomes a practical test of whether a stated priority is real.
The ONE Thing|Gary Keller & Jay Papasan.author: Gary Keller co-founded Keller Williams Realty. He and editor Jay Papasan drew on work with business owners whose many apparent priorities competed for the same hours.

The Outsiders|William N. Thorndike Jr..brief: Eight CEOs made their mark through quiet decisions about where the next dollar should go.
The Outsiders|William N. Thorndike Jr..synopsis: Thorndike studies buybacks, acquisitions, dividends and reinvestment across very different businesses. The comparisons treat allocation of cash as a central part of the chief executive's job.
The Outsiders|William N. Thorndike Jr..author: William Thorndike founded the investment firm Housatonic Partners. He approached the executives as an investor trying to explain long-run returns that ordinary management profiles missed.

The Personal MBA|Josh Kaufman.brief: Kaufman organizes the basic workings of a business into concepts a reader can study independently.
The Personal MBA|Josh Kaufman.synopsis: Value creation, sales and finance sit alongside decisions about people and systems. The short entries let a reader look up the part of a business they need to understand next.
The Personal MBA|Josh Kaufman.author: Josh Kaufman developed his reading project while working at Procter & Gamble. He expanded it into an alternative course of independent study for people considering business school.

The Replaceable Founder|Ari Meisel.brief: Meisel asks how a business would operate if its founder could no longer answer every question.
The Replaceable Founder|Ari Meisel.synopsis: He follows recurring work through simplification, automation and delegation. The aim is for the next person to know both what to do and when they have authority to decide.
The Replaceable Founder|Ari Meisel.author: Ari Meisel founded Less Doing and coached entrepreneurs on reducing their involvement in routine operations. This book concentrates that work on a founder's dependence on being available.

The Richest Man in Babylon|George S. Cla.brief: Clason uses parables set in ancient Babylon to explain saving, lending and spending.
The Richest Man in Babylon|George S. Cla.synopsis: Characters who earn similar wages find themselves in different financial circumstances. Their conversations introduce the practice of keeping part of one's earnings and questioning an investment one does not understand.
The Richest Man in Babylon|George S. Cla.author: George Clason published financial pamphlets that banks and insurance companies distributed to customers. Their compact parables later became the book.

The Sales Acceleration Formula|Mark Robe.brief: Roberge asks whether building a sales team can be made as systematic as building a product.
The Sales Acceleration Formula|Mark Robe.synopsis: He follows the work in sequence, beginning with who gets hired and how those hires are trained. Sales data then helps a manager see where the process itself needs attention.
The Sales Acceleration Formula|Mark Robe.author: Mark Roberge trained as an engineer and led sales at HubSpot during its early growth. The hiring and training systems in the book grew out of that job.

The Sales Advantage|Dale Carnegie.brief: A practical guide to discovering what a customer wants before asking for an order.
The Sales Advantage|Dale Carnegie.synopsis: The book follows preparation, questioning and listening through to handling concerns. It applies Carnegie's lessons about human relationships to the particular demands of a sales conversation.
The Sales Advantage|Dale Carnegie.author: J. Oliver Crom and Michael Crom wrote the book from Dale Carnegie Training's sales courses. The Carnegie name on the shelf refers to that teaching tradition.

The Sales Development Playbook|Trish Ber.brief: Bertuzzi works through the decisions involved in building a team that starts sales conversations.
The Sales Development Playbook|Trish Ber.synopsis: The book examines whom to target, how to structure a role and what managers should measure. A team can log a great deal of outreach without creating an opportunity the next salesperson can use.
The Sales Development Playbook|Trish Ber.author: Trish Bertuzzi founded The Bridge Group and advised business-to-business sales teams. Her examples come from companies deciding how much specialization their sales process could support.

The Sales Playbook for Founders|YC Start.brief: A founder's guide to moving a business customer from an initial conversation to a signed deal.
The Sales Playbook for Founders|YC Start.synopsis: The Startup School talk covers qualifying prospects and keeping a sales process moving. It treats an enthusiastic meeting as an intermediate step whose value depends on what the customer agrees to do next.
The Sales Playbook for Founders|YC Start.author: YC's Tom Blomfield founded GoCardless and Monzo. He draws on selling financial products to businesses before an established name could open the door for him.

The Science of Getting Rich|Wallace D. W.brief: Wattles presents prosperity as a discipline of thought and action in the New Thought tradition.
The Science of Getting Rich|Wallace D. W.synopsis: He argues that a person can pursue wealth creatively and asks readers to practise gratitude and purposeful work. The title uses the language of his philosophy rather than that of an experimental study.
The Science of Getting Rich|Wallace D. W.author: Wallace D. Wattles was an American New Thought writer. The book appeared in 1910, when spiritual accounts of prosperity had a substantial popular readership.

The Score Takes Care of Itself|Bill Wals.brief: Walsh explains the standards he set before the 49ers became a winning team.
The Score Takes Care of Itself|Bill Wals.synopsis: Practice routines, office conduct and the wording of instructions all enter his account of coaching. A score records a result after the game, while these are choices a coach can make beforehand.
The Score Takes Care of Itself|Bill Wals.author: Bill Walsh coached San Francisco to three Super Bowl wins. Steve Jamison and Walsh's son Craig helped bring his teaching and recollections together in a book published after his death.

The Snowball|Alice Schroeder.brief: Schroeder traces Warren Buffett's investing life alongside the family relationships that shaped it.
The Snowball|Alice Schroeder.synopsis: Childhood businesses give way to investment partnerships and Berkshire Hathaway. The biography follows the accumulation of money while asking what the demands of that work meant at home.
The Snowball|Alice Schroeder.author: Alice Schroeder covered Berkshire as an insurance analyst. Buffett granted her extensive access for the biography, and she also interviewed relatives and business associates.

The Sovereign Individual|James Dale Davi.brief: Davidson and Rees-Mogg predict how digital networks could alter the balance between states and individuals.
The Sovereign Individual|James Dale Davi.synopsis: The authors reason from earlier shifts in military and economic technology to a future of more mobile wealth. Reading it today also means reading a late-1990s forecast made before many of those technologies were commonplace.
The Sovereign Individual|James Dale Davi.author: James Dale Davidson wrote about investment and politics. William Rees-Mogg edited The Times and wrote on public affairs. Their collaboration brings both perspectives to the forecast.

The Startup Playbook|David Kidder.brief: Kidder interviews founders about the early choices they still consider decisive.
The Startup Playbook|David Kidder.synopsis: Rather than tell one company's history, he asks entrepreneurs to revisit hiring, products and moments when the original plan failed. Differences among the answers are part of the value of the collection.
The Startup Playbook|David Kidder.author: David Kidder was a startup founder himself. His interviews approach well-known companies through the questions one entrepreneur might ask another.

The Startup of You|Reid Hoffman & Ben Ca.brief: Hoffman and Casnocha treat a career as a venture whose assumptions need updating.
The Startup of You|Reid Hoffman & Ben Ca.synopsis: They examine professional networks, opportunities and backup plans. An alternative plan has value even when the original one works because it helps a person decide which risks they can afford.
The Startup of You|Reid Hoffman & Ben Ca.author: Reid Hoffman co-founded LinkedIn. Ben Casnocha founded a company while still in school. Their different starting points inform a book about working in a changing employment market.

The Value of Debt in Building Wealth|Tho.brief: Anderson asks when paying down every debt can leave a household short of cash it needs.
The Value of Debt in Building Wealth|Tho.synopsis: He weighs the cost of borrowing against liquidity and the demands of different stages of life. The tradeoffs depend on the terms of the debt and the household's ability to withstand a setback.
The Value of Debt in Building Wealth|Tho.author: Thomas J. Anderson worked in wealth management and wrote a series on how borrowers use debt. He approached the question from conversations about clients' entire balance sheets.

The Way of The Superior Man|David Deida.brief: Deida writes about the tensions between purpose, intimacy and desire in a man's life.
The Way of The Superior Man|David Deida.synopsis: Short chapters address how a man might stay present with a partner while retaining direction in his own work. The book develops these ideas through the author's spiritual framework of masculine and feminine energies.
The Way of The Superior Man|David Deida.author: David Deida writes and teaches about sexuality and intimate relationships. This work belongs to that spiritual teaching tradition and reflects its particular language about gender.

The Way of the Wolf|Jordan Belfort.brief: Belfort sets out the sales script and delivery techniques he calls the Straight Line.
The Way of the Wolf|Jordan Belfort.synopsis: The book follows a call from the opening seconds through objections and a request for commitment. Belfort gives particular weight to the salesperson's voice and the listener's confidence.
The Way of the Wolf|Jordan Belfort.author: Jordan Belfort ran Stratton Oakmont and was convicted of securities fraud. He later taught sales, a relevant piece of context for a book on the persuasive methods he used.

The Winner Effect|Ian Robertson.brief: Robertson asks how winning once can change a person's behavior the next time they compete.
The Winner Effect|Ian Robertson.synopsis: He looks at the interaction between confidence, power and physiology, drawing on studies of humans and other animals. The same changes that encourage action can also distort judgment.
The Winner Effect|Ian Robertson.author: Ian Robertson is a clinical psychologist and neuroscientist who worked at Trinity College Dublin. He brought research on brain and behavior to a subject often told through winners' biographies.

The Work of Art|Adam Moss.brief: Moss asks artists to reconstruct the making of one particular work.
The Work of Art|Adam Moss.synopsis: Drafts, sketches and abandoned versions sit beside conversations about the choices that survived. A finished lyric or a painting becomes a record of revisions that its audience would normally never see.
The Work of Art|Adam Moss.author: Adam Moss edited New York magazine. After leaving that job and trying to paint, he became interested in how other people moved through the uncertain middle of making something.

Think and Grow Rich|Napoleon Hill.brief: Hill sets out a philosophy of achievement built around a definite purpose and sustained effort.
Think and Grow Rich|Napoleon Hill.synopsis: The book pairs exercises in goal setting and self-suggestion with stories drawn from American business. Its argument about thought and wealth belongs to the self-help culture of the Depression years.
Think and Grow Rich|Napoleon Hill.author: Napoleon Hill published the book in 1937. He presented his work through accounts of successful industrialists, an approach that shaped generations of business self-help writing.

Think like a Rocket Scientist|Ozan Varol.brief: Varol uses the habits of space exploration to rethink decisions made with incomplete information.
Think like a Rocket Scientist|Ozan Varol.synopsis: He examines working from first principles, running tests that could disprove a favored idea and learning from failure. Mission examples give those instructions concrete consequences.
Think like a Rocket Scientist|Ozan Varol.author: Ozan Varol worked on the operations team for the Mars Exploration Rovers before becoming a law professor. He drew on both engineering and teaching to write the book.

Thinking Fast and Slow|Daniel Kahneman.brief: Kahneman examines the judgments people make before they realize they have made a judgment.
Thinking Fast and Slow|Daniel Kahneman.synopsis: Experiments in probability and choice show how an easy question can stand in for the difficult one actually being asked. Later chapters consider how people remember experiences and weigh gains against losses.
Thinking Fast and Slow|Daniel Kahneman.author: Daniel Kahneman developed much of this research with Amos Tversky. He wrote the book late in his career, looking back on the experiments and the friendship behind them.

Thinking in Bets|Annie Duke.brief: A good poker player can play the right hand and still lose the pot.
Thinking in Bets|Annie Duke.synopsis: A well-played hand can lose. She applies that lesson to estimating probabilities, reviewing decisions and talking with people who can challenge a confident opinion.
Thinking in Bets|Annie Duke.author: Annie Duke played professional poker after studying cognitive psychology. At the table, the information a player never gets to see is often as important as the cards they do.

Thou Shall Prosper|Rabbi Daniel Lapin.brief: Lapin approaches earning a living through Jewish teachings about trade and service.
Thou Shall Prosper|Rabbi Daniel Lapin.synopsis: He connects trust, specialization and business relationships with questions of moral obligation. Readers meet an explicitly religious account of why commercial activity can contribute to a community.
Thou Shall Prosper|Rabbi Daniel Lapin.author: Daniel Lapin is a rabbi who writes and speaks about business ethics. He structures the book around principles he draws from Jewish religious tradition.

Total Recall|Arnold Schwarzenegger.brief: Schwarzenegger recounts the decisions that carried him from rural Austria into three very public careers.
Total Recall|Arnold Schwarzenegger.synopsis: Bodybuilding contests give way to Hollywood and electoral politics. The memoir sets meticulous training and career planning beside accounts of family life and his failures as a husband.
Total Recall|Arnold Schwarzenegger.author: Arnold Schwarzenegger wrote after serving two terms as governor of California. He could look back on pursuing each new career while still identified publicly with the last one.

Traction|Gino Wickman.brief: Wickman gives a leadership team a common way to run its weekly business.
Traction|Gino Wickman.synopsis: His Entrepreneurial Operating System brings goals, responsibilities, measurements and problem-solving into a regular meeting rhythm. The book includes the working documents teams use to put it into practice.
Traction|Gino Wickman.author: Gino Wickman ran a family business and later advised entrepreneurial companies. He developed the system by working repeatedly with owners and their leadership teams.

Traffic Secrets|Russell Brunson.brief: Brunson starts with the places potential customers already spend their attention.
Traffic Secrets|Russell Brunson.synopsis: He works through borrowed audiences, paid traffic and contacts a business can reach directly. The longer-term question is how to keep reaching customers when a platform changes its rules.
Traffic Secrets|Russell Brunson.author: Russell Brunson wrote this as the traffic volume of his marketing series. Running ClickFunnels put him close to sellers whose results depended on search engines, ads and mailing lists.

Trillion Dollar Coach|Eric Schmidt, Jona.brief: Colleagues remember the coaching of Bill Campbell, a quiet presence behind several Silicon Valley leaders.
Trillion Dollar Coach|Eric Schmidt, Jona.synopsis: The book reconstructs one-to-one meetings, arguments and the ways Campbell helped executives work together. Many of his interventions took place outside the formal reporting structure.
Trillion Dollar Coach|Eric Schmidt, Jona.author: Eric Schmidt, Jonathan Rosenberg and Alan Eagle knew Campbell through Google. They interviewed others after his death to record coaching that had largely happened in private.

Unlimited Power|Tony Robbins.brief: Robbins presents exercises for changing the mental and physical state a person brings to a task.
Unlimited Power|Tony Robbins.synopsis: He asks readers to model effective performers and experiment with posture, language and attention. The methods reflect his early interest in neuro-linguistic programming.
Unlimited Power|Tony Robbins.author: Tony Robbins published the book during his early career as a motivational trainer. Its exercises reflect the live seminars through which he first built an audience.

Unlock Secrets|Russell Brunson.brief: A companion workbook for putting Brunson's three Secrets books to use together.
Unlock Secrets|Russell Brunson.synopsis: The workbook connects exercises on building a sales funnel, explaining an offer and finding traffic. It is intended to be filled in alongside the main books as a reader works through a business of their own.
Unlock Secrets|Russell Brunson.author: Russell Brunson described Unlock Secrets as the workbook linking DotCom Secrets, Expert Secrets and Traffic Secrets. That role explains its place beside three similarly titled books on this shelf.

Unscripted|MJ DeMarco.brief: DeMarco questions the conventional script of exchanging most of one's working life for a distant retirement.
Unscripted|MJ DeMarco.synopsis: He returns to business ownership and asks what would make a product useful enough to pay its creator repeatedly. The discussion connects ideas about independence with the work of building and selling something.
Unscripted|MJ DeMarco.author: MJ DeMarco built an online limousine marketplace. He wrote this after The Millionaire Fastlane to develop the broader argument about work and autonomy behind his earlier book.

Unshackled: Visa Opportunities for Inter.brief: A library entry on the visa choices facing international students and scholars in the United States.
Unshackled: Visa Opportunities for Inter.synopsis: A published guide called Unshackled follows skilled immigrants through the US immigration system. Its subtitle and byline differ from this shelf record, so the two editions cannot confidently be identified as the same work.
Unshackled: Visa Opportunities for Inter.author: The shelf credits Sharon He. Soundarya Basubramani and immigration attorney Sameer Khedekar wrote the published guide, drawing on immigrant experiences and legal practice.

What Every Real Estate Investor Needs To.brief: Gallinelli shows how the same property can look attractive or expensive depending on the measure used.
What Every Real Estate Investor Needs To.synopsis: Worked examples move through cash flow, capitalization rates and returns over time. The book asks readers to inspect the rent, expenses and financing assumptions underneath a promising number.
What Every Real Estate Investor Needs To.author: Frank Gallinelli founded RealData, which develops real estate investment analysis software. His teaching and software work both required making the arithmetic of property decisions explicit.

Who Moved My Cheese|Spencer Johnson.brief: Four characters return to a familiar supply of cheese and discover it is gone.
Who Moved My Cheese|Spencer Johnson.synopsis: Johnson uses the different reactions inside the maze to ask how people notice and respond to change. The story is deliberately short enough for a group to read and discuss together.
Who Moved My Cheese|Spencer Johnson.author: Spencer Johnson trained as a physician and coauthored The One Minute Manager. He used short fables to give workplace conversations a shared point of reference.

Why Startups Fail|Tom Eisenmann.brief: Eisenmann studies startups that failed even though the usual ingredients for success seemed to be present.
Why Startups Fail|Tom Eisenmann.synopsis: Case histories distinguish different patterns of failure, including a promising launch that hides weak demand. He also examines what a founder can do when preserving the company is no longer the right goal.
Why Startups Fail|Tom Eisenmann.author: Tom Eisenmann taught entrepreneurship at Harvard Business School. Failures among founders he knew prompted him to investigate what standard startup advice had failed to explain.

Why We Sleep|Matthew Walker.brief: Walker describes what happens in the brain and body across a night's sleep.
Why We Sleep|Matthew Walker.synopsis: Chapters follow sleep stages, dreaming and the effects of disrupted rest. The book argues for treating sleep as a biological necessity and brings the author's interpretation of research to a general audience.
Why We Sleep|Matthew Walker.author: Matthew Walker is a sleep researcher and professor at UC Berkeley. Laboratory studies of memory and sleep form part of the scientific background to his account.

Winners|Alastair Campbell.brief: Campbell interviews competitors and leaders about how they prepare for the result everyone else sees.
Winners|Alastair Campbell.synopsis: Sport sits alongside business and politics. The conversations examine preparation, setbacks and the role a team plays in achievements normally credited to one person.
Winners|Alastair Campbell.author: Alastair Campbell worked as a journalist and as Tony Blair's communications director. Political campaigns gave him firsthand experience of a contest with a public result and an immovable deadline.

Wisdom Takes Work|Ryan Holiday.brief: Holiday treats wisdom as something acquired through study, attention and the correction of mistakes.
Wisdom Takes Work|Ryan Holiday.synopsis: Historical lives supply the cases. The emphasis falls on the effort behind a sound judgment, especially the work of reconsidering something one once felt certain about.
Wisdom Takes Work|Ryan Holiday.author: Ryan Holiday wrote this as the wisdom installment of his series on the four classical virtues, following books on courage, temperance and justice.

Wooden on Leadership|John Wooden.brief: Wooden describes the daily teaching behind UCLA's record in college basketball.
Wooden on Leadership|John Wooden.synopsis: Practice plans, preparation and standards of behavior receive as much attention as games. His Pyramid of Success gives those details a structure he could explain to a new player.
Wooden on Leadership|John Wooden.author: John Wooden coached UCLA to ten NCAA men's basketball titles. He worked with Steve Jamison to set down lessons from decades of coaching.

Work With The Best|Jay Yang.brief: Yang explains how to approach someone you would like to work for with evidence that you can already help.
Work With The Best|Jay Yang.synopsis: The guide moves from researching a person's work to making something useful before asking for a meeting. Its examples concern the first opportunity, when a conventional résumé offers little proof.
Work With The Best|Jay Yang.author: Jay Yang used a cold email to land an internship at newsletter company beehiiv. That experience supplies a concrete starting point for the advice he gives early-career readers.

You Can Just Do Things|Jay Yang.brief: Yang asks what a young person can start doing before anyone gives them permission.
You Can Just Do Things|Jay Yang.synopsis: He focuses on small acts of initiative, including contacting people and beginning work without a formal invitation. The aim is to make the first attempt concrete enough to do today.
You Can Just Do Things|Jay Yang.author: Jay Yang built early work opportunities through unsolicited outreach and writing online. He uses those experiences to address readers who have more curiosity than credentials.

You Can Negotiate Anything|Herb Cohen.brief: Cohen looks at the information, time and perceived power on either side of an everyday negotiation.
You Can Negotiate Anything|Herb Cohen.synopsis: He examines deadlines, preparation and the things each side cares about that the other might not suspect. Familiar transactions give readers a way to try the ideas outside a formal bargaining room.
You Can Negotiate Anything|Herb Cohen.author: Herb Cohen trained negotiators and advised businesses and government organizations. He wrote for the person who negotiates regularly without being given that job title.

Zero to One|Peter Thiel.brief: Thiel asks what it takes to build a company that does something genuinely new.
Zero to One|Peter Thiel.synopsis: The book examines small initial markets, proprietary technology and the advantages of escaping direct competition. It asks founders to explain what they believe about the world that their rivals have missed.
Zero to One|Peter Thiel.author: Peter Thiel taught a startup course at Stanford after co-founding PayPal. Blake Masters's class notes became the starting point for the book they wrote together.
